title: Steel Front Bumper — Budget Through Premium Options

parts.name: Smittybilt XRC Comp Series Front Bumper (JL)

citations.title: Warn Ascent JL Front Bumper Product Page
Fab Four Stubby JL Bumper Overview
Rugged Ridge Spartan Bumper JL

summary: The JL's factory front fascia is plastic and won't survive a significant trail hit — a steel bumper is the foundation of any trail-ready build, and the right choice depends heavily on whether your rig has front parking sensors.
description:
The JL Wrangler introduced front parking sensors on certain trims and packages — specifically, the Sahara with the Safety & Security Group and any JL equipped with the Park Assist package. These sensors sit in the factory plastic fascia and disappear when you swap to a steel bumper. Some aftermarket bumpers are designed to accommodate the factory sensors with integrated sensor ports; others are not. Before ordering any bumper, pull your window sticker or check the Uconnect settings screen to confirm whether your JL has front sensors. If it does, verify explicitly that your chosen bumper is sensor-compatible or accept that the sensors will become non-functional.

The Smittybilt XRC Comp at $499 is the entry-level choice with a winch-ready plate welded in. The construction is heavier gauge than the factory fascia but lighter than the mid-range and premium bumpers — adequate for trail use that doesn't regularly involve direct rock contact. If your budget tops out here, it's a functional platform. The Rugged Ridge Spartan at $549 is the other budget-accessible option; similar gauge to the Smittybilt with a slightly more refined design and sensor port provisions on most variants.

The Warn Ascent at $999 is the value-to-quality sweet spot for most JL builds. Warn's bumper engineering is done in-house and the Ascent is designed specifically around Warn winch mounting dimensions — if you're running a Warn VR EVO or Zeon, the fit is precise. The Ascent also provides better approach angle than most stubby designs while maintaining a lower front profile that keeps headlight sightlines intact.

The Fab Four Stubby at $1,399 is the premium choice for rock-build rigs where approach angle is critical. The stubby design removes the outer wings of the factory bumper envelope entirely, dramatically improving the approach angle — the difference is visible and meaningful on off-camber approaches. The tradeoff is reduced frontal protection on the outer edges and no parking sensor provision. Fab Four's fabrication quality is excellent and the finish holds up well.
steps: Disconnect the negative battery terminal before starting — parking sensor wiring and any ambient temperature sensor leads need to be disconnected safely.

Remove the factory plastic front fascia. Most JL fascias are held by push-pin retainers along the top edge, two bolts in the wheel wells, and clips along the lower valance. A trim panel tool and patience beats a screwdriver and frustration here.
Disconnect all sensor connectors attached to the factory fascia — parking sensors, fog light harnesses, ambient temperature sensor. Label connectors before unplugging.
Remove the factory crash bar/impact absorber. This bolts to the frame horns with four bolts.
If the bumper kit includes a fog light relocation bracket or sensor housing, install it now before the bumper goes on.
With a helper, lift the new bumper into position and start all bolts finger-tight.
Confirm bumper is square to the vehicle before torquing. Small asymmetries become obvious at distance.
Torque mounting hardware to manufacturer spec — typically 60–80 ft-lb on the main frame mount bolts.
Reconnect fog lights, relocate parking sensor harnesses to bumper sensor ports if present.
If running a winch: mount winch before final bumper install when possible — much easier than fishing the fairlead through the bumper opening after the fact.
Reconnect battery, test all lights and sensor functions.
pros: Steel construction provides protection that factory plastic cannot — trail-going JLs should have a steel bumper
Most options in this range include a winch-ready plate — a significant value-add given winch mounting hardware complexity
Warn Ascent's purpose-built compatibility with Warn winches eliminates fitment guesswork
Fab Four Stubby approach-angle improvement is meaningful on technical trails
Rugged Ridge and Smittybilt options deliver core protection at accessible price points
cons: Parking sensor compatibility must be verified before purchase — this is the most common ordering mistake on JL bumper installs
Full-width steel bumpers add 50–90 lbs to the front end, affecting steering feel and approach weight
Premium options (Fab Four, Warn) represent significant investment — budget total build cost including winch before committing to top-tier bumper
Stubby designs sacrifice outer approach protection for angle — not ideal for builds that see frequent brush or trail debris
Factory fog lights typically require relocation hardware (sometimes sold separately) — verify what's included

summary: The stock JL rear bumper is plastic, and the factory swing-arm tire carrier was not built to handle a 37" spare — a steel rear bumper with a proper tire carrier is one of the most functional upgrades on a trail-going JL.
description:
The JL Wrangler ships with a plastic rear fascia and a factory swing-arm carrier that's rated for the 32"–33" factory spare. When you move to 35s or 37s, the added weight of a larger, heavier tire pushes the factory swing arm beyond its design intent — the pivot bearing wears prematurely, the carrier droops, and the rear closure becomes misaligned over time. A steel rear bumper with an integrated, purpose-built carrier solves all of this at once.

The Smittybilt XRC at $899 is the value entry point. The construction is functional, the carrier pivot is substantially more robust than factory, and it handles up to a 35" spare with confidence. For 37s, the Smittybilt's carrier is on the lighter-duty end of capable — it will hold the spare, but the pivot bearing load is higher than with premium options. If you're running 37s long-term, the Poison Spyder, LOD, or Warn units are better investments.

Poison Spyder's rear bumper at $1,199 is the mid-premium choice — heavier construction than the Smittybilt, a more robust pivot mechanism, and finishes that hold up better over time. LOD's Destroyer at $1,399 is notably thick-plate construction with a functional minimalist design that doesn't sacrifice departure angle significantly. The Warn Ascent at $1,599 is the top-tier option: Warn's engineering is thorough, and the carrier pivot mechanism on the Ascent has the smoothest operation and longest expected service life of the four options.

**Hitch integration:** Most JL rear bumpers include a 2" receiver hitch as part of the design. Verify hitch integration before purchasing if you run a trailer, bike rack, or recovery equipment off the rear. The factory Class II hitch (if equipped) is removed during bumper install.

**37" spare weight:** A mounted 37x12.5R17 on a steel wheel weighs approximately 85–95 lbs. The tire carrier pivot and the frame attachment points need to handle that load over rough terrain — lighter-duty carriers are not suited to this use case. Go heavier-duty than you think you need.
steps: Remove the factory plastic rear fascia (push-pin retainers, clips along the underside, wheel well bolts).
Disconnect the rear license plate light harness and any backup sensor harnesses.
If factory-equipped with a trailer hitch receiver, remove it. The new bumper's hitch replaces it.
Remove the factory swing-arm spare tire carrier — typically four bolts on the factory hinge assembly.
Remove the factory rear impact absorber/crash bar (bolts to the rear frame rails).
With a helper, lift the new rear bumper assembly into position. These assemblies are heavy — a 37" spare carrier with bumper can exceed 100 lbs unloaded.
Start all mounting bolts finger-tight, then confirm the bumper is level and centered before torquing.
Torque mounting hardware to manufacturer spec — typically 60–80 ft-lb on main frame bolts.
Reinstall license plate light using the new bracket (usually included). Reconnect harnesses.
Relocate rear backup sensors if applicable and bumper provides sensor ports.
Load the spare tire onto the new carrier, confirm pivot operation swings freely and latch engages cleanly.
Check departure angle clearance — lower the vehicle fully, then drive over a rolled curb or use a ramp to verify the new bumper profile doesn't contact prematurely.
pros: Dramatically more robust tire carrier than factory — purpose-built for 35"–37" spare weight
Steel construction protects the rear frame area during recovery and trail impacts
Integrated 2" hitch receiver on most designs adds functional utility
Departure angle on most JL rear bumpers is improved over factory or equal — the low rear fascia of the JL is typically the departure bottleneck, not the bumper
Full-replacement install removes all factory plastic from the rear — cleaner visual result
cons: Total assembly weight (bumper + spare on carrier) adds significant mass to the rear — up to 100–120 lbs beyond factory. This affects rear spring rate and body pitch
Installation requires two people — these assemblies are too heavy and unwieldy for solo mounting
Factory backup sensors require relocation or sacrifice — verify what your chosen bumper does with sensor provision
Premium options (Warn, LOD, Poison Spyder) represent significant investment — budget realistically against front bumper and other armor priorities
Smittybilt XRC is functional for 35s but not the ideal choice for long-term 37" spare loads — carrier pivot will see accelerated wear

title: Skid Plate Kit — Engine, Transfer Case, and Fuel Tank
tools_required: pry bar (for stubborn existing skid alignment)

summary: The JL's underbody layout is different enough from the JK's that JK skids will not fit — this is not a fitment approximation, it's a flat incompatibility. Every skid plate on a JL must be JL-spec.
description:
Jeep updated the JL's frame geometry, crossmember locations, and underbody component placement significantly compared to the JK. The oil pan position, transfer case mounting, and fuel tank skid integration points all moved. If you have JK skids in your garage, they are not transferable. This is worth knowing before buying used parts.

The JL Rubicon ships with a factory aluminum skid package that provides basic coverage — better than nothing, but thin and prone to deformation on genuine rock contact. The Sport and Sahara have no factory skids worth mentioning. Aftermarket steel skids address both the coverage gaps and the material upgrade.

The Teraflex JL skid kit at $499 covers the primary three: the transfer case belly area, the engine/oil pan, and the front crossmember. It's 3/16" steel plate, laser-cut for JL-specific fitment, and the mount points align with factory hardware. This is the most popular mid-range option because the price is fair and the coverage addresses the components most commonly damaged on trail.

Rock Hard 4x4's JL system at $699 adds coverage to the areas the Teraflex kit leaves exposed — specifically the rear areas near the fuel tank and the front diff on equipped trims. The extra coverage is worth the $200 premium if your trails involve sustained belly exposure rather than occasional hits. GenRight's full underbelly kit at $899 is the comprehensive choice for rock-crawl builds — every vulnerable surface has plate coverage, and the kit is designed to work as a unified deflection surface rather than individual plates with gaps.

Rubicon Express at $449 is the value option — slightly thinner plate than Rock Hard, adequate for mild to moderate trail use, and competitively priced. For a JL that's primarily an overland rig with occasional trail excursions, the Rubicon Express kit is a defensible choice.
steps: Lift the vehicle on jack stands at the frame rails — you need clear underbody access to work comfortably.
If factory plastic undertray or factory aluminum skids are present, remove them. Factory aluminum Rubicon skids unbolt cleanly; factory plastic undertrays use a combination of bolts and push pins.
Inspect the underbody for existing damage before installing new skids — address any compromised brackets or crossmember sections before covering them.
Dry-fit all skid plates before starting installation. Confirm mounting hole alignment with factory threaded inserts or frame holes.
Start all hardware finger-tight before torquing any individual plate. Multiple plates often share mounting points, and a plate torqued early will bind adjacent plates.
Torque all hardware to manufacturer spec — typically 30–45 ft-lb depending on bolt size and material.
Confirm clearance around exhaust components if your kit covers the area near the cat or mid-pipe. Aftermarket skids occasionally require minor exhaust hanger relocation.
pros: Protects the JL's most vulnerable underbody components — oil pan, transfer case, and fuel tank contacts are what end trail days
Bolt-on installation; no cutting or welding required for any of the kits listed
Teraflex and Rock Hard kits provide better coverage than the factory Rubicon aluminum skids at similar or lower cost
Steel plate construction deflects and slides over rock contact rather than deforming and catching
GenRight full kit eliminates all coverage gaps — appropriate for builds that prioritize underbody protection
cons: JK skids are completely incompatible — do not attempt JK fitment on a JL regardless of appearance similarity
Steel skid weight adds to unsprung/belly weight — full kits add 40–80 lbs total
Factory Rubicon aluminum skids are not compatible with most aftermarket kits as supplements — plan for full replacement
GenRight's $899 kit is a significant investment; prioritize by terrain type before committing to full coverage
Skid plates that have been heavily impacted should be inspected for deformation that could contact exhaust or drivetrain components

title: Rock Sliders and Rocker Guards

parts.name: Poison Spyder JL Rocker Knockers Rock Sliders
Rock Hard 4x4 Patriot Series Rock Sliders (JL)
LOD Offroad Destroyer Series Rock Sliders (JL)

citations.title: Poison Spyder JL Rock Sliders Product Page
Rock Hard 4x4 JL Wrangler Sliders

summary: The rocker panels on the JL Wrangler are exposed — no factory protection — and a single high-centering on a rock shelf can fold sheet metal that costs $600+ to repair. A slider is the single cheapest per-dollar piece of trail insurance available for this platform.
description:
The JL's unibody construction changes how sliders attach compared to the body-on-frame XJ. Sliders for the JL bolt through the body and into the integrated frame rails in the sill area — a robust mounting approach when done correctly, but one that requires precise fit and correct torque specs. Do not attempt to run a JK slider on a JL; the mounting points are different and a slider that's not properly attached to the structure will transfer impact forces to the wrong part of the body.

Poison Spyder's Rocker Knockers are the premium option — heavy-gauge DOM tube construction with a textured powdercoat finish and a step tube design that doubles as a rock step. The $699 price reflects the material quality, but these are genuinely trail-proven hardware. If your build sees regular technical terrain, the Poison Spyder units are worth the premium.

Rock Hard 4x4 is the value-focused choice that doesn't compromise on structural integrity. At $449, the Patriot Series sliders are 3/16" plate with 1.75" DOM tube construction — heavy enough to protect the rockers without the price of premium brands. These are a popular choice for trail builds on a budget. LOD's Destroyer series sits in the middle — $649 for notably thick plate construction and a relatively minimal profile that doesn't add much departure-angle penalty. The Smittybilt XRC sliders at $499 are the budget-ceiling option: adequate construction, lighter gauge than the Rock Hard or LOD, but a functional choice for mild-to-moderate trail use.

**JL vs JLU fitment:** The 2-door JL and 4-door JLU have different wheelbase and rocker lengths. Every manufacturer makes separate part numbers for JL and JLU — verify before ordering. Running a JL-spec slider on a JLU will leave rear coverage gaps; running a JLU slider on a JL won't fit at all.
steps: Chock wheels, lift vehicle on jack stands at the frame rails with enough clearance to work under the rocker area.
Clean the mounting surfaces — factory undercoating and debris on the bolt hole areas will affect seat quality.
Dry-fit both sliders before drilling any pilot holes or running any hardware. The fit should align with the body before torquing.
For bolt-through installations: drill pilot holes per the manufacturer's template if provided. Use sharp bits — the factory sill material is hard.
Install mounting hardware from the inside of the vehicle where required. Some slider designs require a helper inside to hold inner-body hardware while you torque from below.
Start all hardware finger-tight before torquing anything.
Use ratchet straps or a helper to hold the slider in alignment during initial torquing — they're heavy and will shift if unsupported.
Torque all fasteners to manufacturer spec. For most JL sliders, this is 35–45 ft-lb on the main mounting points.
Articulate the doors to confirm clearance — sliders close to the door bottoms need a clearance check before driving.
pros: Protects the most vulnerable body panel on a trail-going JL — rocker damage is expensive and common
Most slider designs double as a step tube, which is a genuine quality-of-life upgrade on a lifted JL
Rock Hard and Smittybilt options deliver real protection at accessible price points
Bolt-on installation (no welding required on any of these options) means a home builder can complete the job
Adds structural rigidity to the sill area — measurable improvement on flex-intensive trail use
cons: JL and JLU require separate part numbers — wrong fitment will not work
Heavy hardware (most sliders add 40–70 lbs) raises the CG slightly and increases unsprung weight
Slider profile affects departure angle — wider, lower-profile sliders sacrifice some departure clearance
Powder coat finish scratches quickly on rocky terrain — expect trail wear; that's what they're for
Smittybilt XRC gauge is lighter than Rock Hard or Poison Spyder; adequate for mild-moderate use but not the choice for serious rock work

parts.name: Mopar Front Diff Cover Gasket / RTV Kit

summary: Service the JL front Dana 44 AdvanTEK every 30,000 miles with 2 quarts of 75W-140 — and know that the FAD housing and stock axle shafts are the two weak points that snap first when you go bigger than 35s.
description:
The JL front axle is a Dana 44 AdvanTEK on Rubicon trims (model M210 wide-track) and an M210 Dana 44-derived front on Sahara/Sport with smaller ring gear. Both share the same housing platform and the same Front Axle Disconnect (FAD) on non-Rubicon trims. The Rubicon's electronic locker lives in this housing. Service fluid is Mopar 75W-140 synthetic GL-5, capacity about 2.0 quarts at the bottom of the fill hole. Change interval is every 30,000 miles under normal driving and every 15,000 miles for vehicles that see water crossings, sand, or regular trail use.

The FAD casting on Sport and Sahara trims is the part to watch. The cast aluminum FAD housing is brittle and is the most common failure point on stock JL fronts, and the plastic FAD coupler bushing inside it wears out and dumps gear oil. If your build is heading past 35-inch tires, the honest move is a FAD-delete with Spicer chromoly inner shafts (PN 10044469 set) — this swaps the plastic coupler for a solid one-piece shaft and gets rid of the disconnect mechanism entirely. Rubicons skip this issue because they came with the locking version and no FAD.

Stock M210 axle shafts are adequate up to 35-inch tires for trail use. Past 35s, especially with lockers and heavy throttle, expect to bend or twist stock shafts within a season or two of hard wheeling. Chromoly upgrades push the working limit to 37-inch tires with the rest of the drivetrain unchanged. An axle truss (Next Venture Motorsports or Artec) adds housing rigidity for builds running 37s+ with lockers — necessary on rigs that see rock crawling, optional for trail rigs.

Ball joints on M210s are a known wear item. Listen for clunks at full lock and inspect for grease weeping at every fluid change. Replace as a set with Synergy or Dynatrac ball joints; the stock joints are unsealed in the lower position and gravel finds its way in.

Aftermarket diff covers (Artec, ARB, Rusty's, AEV) add about 4 ounces of capacity and a magnetic drain plug. They protect the housing on rocks and make fluid changes cleaner because of the drain plug — the stock cover requires you to pull the whole cover to drain.
steps: Park on level ground, warm the axle by driving 5–10 miles so the old fluid drains cleanly.
Position drain pan under the diff cover. Crack the fill plug (top of cover, 3/8" square drive) FIRST to confirm it backs out — if it's stuck and you've already drained, you can't refill.

If you have an aftermarket cover with a drain plug, pull the plug and drain. Otherwise, loosen the cover bolts in a crisscross pattern, leave the top two snug, and pry the bottom of the cover loose to drain.
Remove the cover, wipe the housing clean, inspect the ring gear teeth for pitting or chipping, and check the magnet for metal chunks (fine paste is normal; chunks are not).
Scrape old RTV off both mating surfaces with a plastic scraper. Wipe with brake cleaner.
Apply 1/4" bead of Mopar gray RTV or equivalent silicone around the cover, going inside the bolt holes. Install cover and torque bolts to 25 ft-lbs in a crisscross pattern.
Wait 30 minutes for RTV to set, then fill through the fill hole until fluid is at the bottom of the threads (about 2 quarts). Reinstall fill plug to 30 ft-lbs.
Drive 20–50 miles and recheck for leaks at the cover and fill plug.
pros: Fluid change is a one-hour job with a $40 parts bill
Service catches FAD wear, ball joint slop, and locker-fluid contamination
Chromoly shaft upgrade is a bolt-in once the axle is open
cons: FAD housing is a known weak point on non-Rubicon trims
Stock shafts bend on 37s+ — plan a chromoly budget if you're going big
Mopar 75W-140 is not cheap and the spec is firm — generic 80W-90 will damage the electric locker on Rubicons

title: Dana 44 AdvanTEK Rear — Locker Options

parts.name: Eaton Performance ELocker — 30-spline D44, 3.73 and lower
ARB Air Locker RD-245 — Dana 44 30-spline w/factory CV

citations.title: Eaton 14234-1 Dana 44 Electric Locker — Quadratec
Eaton 14313-2 35 Spline D44/M220 E-Locker — OffRoad Elements
Eaton 19977-010 4-Pinion ELocker 30-spline D44 — Quadratec

summary: Non-Rubicon JLs have an open Dana 44 M220 rear axle that benefits enormously from a locker; Eaton's 14234-1 ELocker is the direct-fit electric answer ($1,100), ARB's RD-245 is the air-actuated alternative if you already run a compressor.
description:
The JL rear axle is a Dana 44 in name only — the housing is the M220 variant, beefier than the front M210 but with its own carrier specs and spline counts. Rubicons come with the OE Tru-Lok electric locker from the factory. Sport, Sport S, Sahara, and Willys come with an open differential (Sahara is sometimes Trac-Lok limited-slip) and a 30- or 32-spline carrier depending on year and gear ratio. Knowing exactly what you have determines which locker fits.

Eaton's ELocker is the most common upgrade because it's electric, one-wire activation, and doesn't require an air compressor. The 14234-1 fits 35-spline M220 carriers on 2018–2023 JL/JT non-Rubicons. The newer 14313-2 covers later model years through 2026. The 19977-010 is the performance 4-pinion option for older 30-spline D44s with 3.73 or numerically lower gears — relevant only if you're running an older D44 conversion or stock gears. Get the spline count from your build sheet or, more reliably, by pulling the diff cover and counting splines on the side gears.

ARB Air Lockers are the air-actuated alternative. The RD-245 fits 30-spline factory-CV Dana 44s and costs $1,091 plus another $340 for the compressor (CKMA12) if you don't have one. Two locker reasons to choose ARB: you want full-open behavior on the street (ELockers are also open until engaged, so this is a wash), and you want the option to add a front ARB later sharing the same compressor. If you're already running OBA for tires, the ARB compressor is a no-cost adder.

Install is not a beginner job. You're pulling the carrier, swapping in the locker, setting pinion preload, ring gear backlash (0.005–0.008"), and pinion bearing crush (~15 in-lb rolling torque used). If you're not regearing at the same time, you can re-use the existing ring gear if it's not worn — but most shops will tell you to regear during the locker install since the carrier is out anyway. If this is your first gear setup, pay a driveline shop. Bad setup eats a $1,100 locker.
steps: Confirm axle: M220 vs older D44, spline count (30/32/35), and current gear ratio (stamped on ring gear or check VIN build sheet).
Drain rear diff fluid. Pull the cover.
Mark and remove the carrier bearing caps. Note shim locations and orientation.
Pry the carrier out. Measure ring-and-pinion backlash before removing anything (note for re-setup).
Press old carrier bearings, install on new locker carrier with same shims to start.
Drop new locker into housing, install bearing caps, torque to spec (55-70 ft-lbs typical).
Re-check backlash (0.005–0.008") and pattern. Adjust shims as needed.
Run actuator wire (ELocker) along axle tube to a frame-mounted switch, or run ARB air line.
Fill diff with 75W-85 or 75W-90 gear oil — Rubicon trac-lok pumpkins also need friction modifier; locker pumpkins do not.
Bench-test actuator before reinstalling driveshaft. Verify locker engages and disengages cleanly.
pros: Eaton ELocker is fully open until engaged — no street manners trade-off
One-wire install, no air system needed for ELocker
ARB shares compressor with front locker if planning both
Massive traction gain on a non-Rubicon JL
cons: $1,100+ for the locker alone, more if regearing
Setup is unforgiving — backlash off by 0.002" eats a ring gear
Need to know your spline count before ordering — wrong locker = restock fee
ARB requires a compressor, more plumbing

parts.name: JL Rubicon M210 front axle assembly (used)

citations.title: Identifying Wranglers and Their Different Axles — Revolution Gear & Axle

summary: A JL Rubicon front Dana 44 (M210) bolts into a Sport or Sahara JL with the right gear ratio match, but it's 1.5" wider per side, comes with a 4.10 final drive, and requires a recalibration before it'll behave on the road.
description:
The JL Rubicon front axle is technically a Dana M210HD — Dana's modern designation for the wide-knuckle, electric-locker variant Jeep ships under Rubicon trims. Non-Rubicon JLs get the narrower M186 (often called Dana 30 internally). The two share suspension mounting points and brake hardware, which is what makes the swap appealing — bolt-pattern compatibility means you're not fabricating brackets.

What does NOT transfer cleanly is the track width and gearing. The Rubicon axle sits 1.5" wider per wheel flange, which pushes the front tires outboard and changes scrub radius. Stock fender flares cover it, but expect rub on full lock. More importantly, Rubicons ship with 4.10 gears; Sports and Saharas typically run 3.45 or 3.73. If the rear axle doesn't get re-geared to match, the transfer case binds and the driveshafts wind up against each other on dry pavement. Either re-gear the rear or plan on swapping both axles as a pair.

The electric locker is the real prize. It engages through the Rubicon-only switch panel, which non-Rubicon JLs don't have. Wiring the locker requires either a salvaged Rubicon dash harness or a standalone controller (sPOD, Switch Pros). AEV's ProCal Snap will tell the BCM about the new axle, gear ratio, and locker so the dashboard and ABS behave normally — without it, expect persistent dash warnings and incorrect speedometer readings.

Driveshaft length is the other gotcha. Rubicon front driveshafts are slightly shorter to match the wider axle pinion offset. Trying to re-use a Sport driveshaft will cause vibration and premature U-joint wear. Source the matching Rubicon driveshaft from the same donor.

Cross-generation note: JL Rubicon axles are NOT interchangeable with JK Rubicon axles. The JL uses a redesigned knuckle, different ball joints, and an updated electronic locker controller. Don't try to mix generations.
steps: Source a complete JL Rubicon front axle assembly with knuckles, hubs, calipers, ABS sensors, and pinion yoke intact.
Confirm gear ratio on the donor matches your rear axle (or plan to re-gear the rear).
Support the JL on jack stands, remove front tires, disconnect ABS, brake lines, sway bar links, and track bar.
Unbolt control arms at the axle and lower the stock axle out.
Position the Rubicon axle, reattach control arms, track bar, and sway bar links.
Reconnect brake lines (use new banjo washers), bleed the system.
Reconnect ABS sensors and the electric locker harness — splice into a Rubicon donor harness or wire to an aftermarket controller.
Use AEV ProCal Snap to write the new axle code and gear ratio to the BCM.
Test on a flat lot in 2WD before hitting trails. Verify ABS, locker engagement, and steering centering.
pros: Factory locker with proper integration
Wider stance improves stability
Stronger axle shafts and ring gear than M186
Mostly bolt-in if donor is complete
cons: Locker wiring is the hard part — plan it before you start
Wider track means new wheels or spacers off the table without rub
Must match rear axle gearing or re-gear both
AEV ProCal required for proper BCM integration

title: Front and Rear Brake Pad Replacement

citations.title: Mopar JL Wrangler brake torque specs — caliper bracket 110 ft-lb, slide pins 26 ft-lb
JL Wrangler Forums: brake pad and rotor part numbers thread

summary: Front pads and rotors take 90 minutes; rears another 60. Caliper bracket bolts are 110 ft-lb, slide pins are 26 ft-lb, lugs are 130 ft-lb. Don't reuse worn slide pin boots — torn boots cause uneven pad wear within 5,000 miles.
description:
JL Wrangler brakes are larger than JK across the lineup — the front rotor went from 12.9" on JK Sport to 13.0" Sport/13.4" Rubicon on JL. The system is otherwise conventional floating caliper with single-piston front and rear. Pad and rotor service is straightforward once you understand the bracket vs slide pin distinction.

**Pad choice.** OE Mopar pads are quiet but dust-heavy. Akebono ACT-series ceramic pads stay clean and bite well below 1,000°F — the right choice for daily-drivers and mild trail use. Hawk LTS gives more cold bite for tow rigs. Avoid no-name pads from auction sites; they'll glaze and squeal within 6 months.

**Rotor decision.** Rotors are sacrificial. If yours have <0.030" of useful thickness left (verify with a micrometer against the minimum stamped on the rotor hat), replace them. Centric Premium and Bosch QuietCast are both quiet and last 50K+ miles. Slotted/drilled rotors look aggressive but offer no benefit for the JL's weight class and crack faster.

**Slide pins matter more than pads.** A torn slide pin boot lets sand and water into the pin bore. The caliper then sticks on one side, the inboard pad wears faster than outboard, and you replace pads at half life. Inspect both pins every brake service. Re-grease with high-temp synthetic brake grease — never wheel bearing grease (it melts).
steps: Loosen lug nuts before lifting. Lift one wheel, support on stand. Remove wheel.
Inspect the caliper for leaks at the dust boot and at the hose fitting. A wet caliper goes in the rebuild pile, not the reinstall pile.
Open the master cylinder cap to let air escape as the pistons retract. (Don't let the reservoir overflow.)
Pull the two 13mm slide pin bolts on the caliper. Lift caliper off the bracket. Hang it from the spring with a wire — never let it hang from the brake hose.
Slide the old pads out of the bracket. Note the wear pattern — uneven wear = stuck slide pin.
Pull the slide pins out of the bracket. Wipe clean. Check the boots — replace if torn. Re-grease with high-temp brake grease and reseat.

(If replacing rotors) Pull the two 15mm bracket bolts and lift bracket off. Remove the rotor (may need a few hammer taps if rust-stuck). Wipe new rotor clean with brake cleaner — they ship with rust preventative oil. Reinstall bracket, 110 ft-lb on bolts.
Insert new pads into the bracket. Apply a thin smear of brake grease on the pad backing where it contacts the caliper piston and the slide ears.
Compress the caliper piston with a C-clamp using an old pad as the contact surface. Push slowly so the master doesn't overflow.
Reinstall caliper over new pads. Torque the 13mm slide pin bolts to 26 ft-lb.
Reinstall wheel. Torque lugs to 130 ft-lb in a star pattern.
**Critical:** Pump the brake pedal 5–10 times before driving to seat the pads against the rotor. The first pedal will go to the floor if you skip this. Verify firm pedal before moving the vehicle.
Re-torque lugs after 50–100 miles.
pros: Standard floating caliper design
Common Akebono / Centric parts at any parts store
90 minutes per axle once you've done it
No special tools beyond a C-clamp
cons: Easy to forget the pedal-pump step (and rear-end someone)
Slide pin neglect = premature pad wear
Larger Rubicon rotors not interchangeable with Sport
Lug torque is high (130 ft-lb) — needs a real torque wrench, not a breaker bar guess

title: Brake Rotor Replacement

parts.name: Mopar OEM front rotor — standard brakes (0.95" thick)
Mopar OEM front rotor — heavy duty brakes (1.1" thick)
Powerstop Z36 rotor + pad kit (front and rear)

citations.title: JL Brake Rotor Sizes and Codes Reference
Mopar 68273502AB Brake Rotor Specifications

summary: JL Wranglers ship with one of three front rotor packages — verify which one you have before ordering. Standard rotors are 0.95" thick (PN 68273502AB), heavy-duty are 1.1" thick (PN 68250085AB). Wrong rotor won't fit. Full job runs 2 hours, $140 OEM front pair or $320 for a full four-corner kit.
description:
The JL Wrangler shipped from the factory with three distinct front brake configurations: BR2/BR3/BR6 packages with 1.1" thick front rotors, and BRY with 0.945" rotors. Standard Sport and Sahara trims got the thinner BRY setup; Rubicon and tow-package trucks got the heavier 1.1" rotors. The bracket and caliper bolt to the same knuckle, but the rotor itself is taller — install the wrong rotor and the pads won't reach.

How to tell which you have without VIN decoding: pop a wheel and measure with a micrometer. Anything 27mm or thicker (new) is heavy-duty. 24mm range is standard. The Mopar build sheet identifies the brake package by code (BR2, BR3, BR6, BRY) but most owners don't have it handy. Measuring is faster than digging up the build sheet.

Rotor wear vs warp: like the JK, the JL front rotors don't tolerate creek crossings well. A glowing rotor dunked in cold water sets the casting slightly out-of-round and you'll feel it as steering-wheel shimmy under braking from highway speeds. Resurfacing rarely lasts more than a single pad cycle. Replace the rotor when warp shows up.

OEM Mopar rotors are mid-grade castings — perfectly adequate for stock use. Powerstop Z36 and EBC Premium upgrade rotors cost the same to a little more and run cooler, which matters for lifted JLs running 35s or for tow rigs. Drilled-and-slotted "performance" rotors offer no real benefit on a sub-5,000-lb vehicle with single-piston calipers — the drill holes become crack initiators after a few hundred heat cycles.

The procedure mirrors the JK closely but with two differences. First, JL caliper slider bolt torque is slightly higher (13–15 ft-lb depending on year), still way lower than the bracket bolts. Second, the JL master cylinder is more sensitive to backflow when you compress the piston — definitely open the reservoir cap and have a rag ready.
steps: Crack lug nuts (19mm), lift the front, support on stands at the frame rails.
Remove front wheels. Note brake package: measure rotor thickness with micrometer to confirm.
Open the brake fluid reservoir cap. Drape a rag.
Remove the two 13mm caliper slider bolts on the back of the caliper. Slide the caliper off and support with a hanger — never let it hang from the brake hose.
Compress the caliper piston back into the caliper bore using a C-clamp and an old pad. Move slowly.
Pull old pads from bracket. Note shim orientation.
Remove the two 18mm caliper bracket bolts at the knuckle. Lift bracket off. Bag it; it's reusable.
Pull the old rotor off the hub. Use M8x1.25 puller-hole bolts if stuck.
Wire-brush the hub face clean. Rust ridges cause runout that returns as pedal pulsing.
Install new rotor (correct thickness for your brake package). Light anti-seize on the hub mating face only — never on the friction surface.
Reinstall bracket and torque bracket bolts to 110 ft-lb.
Install new pads if pad life is below 5mm. Apply light brake grease to pad backs and slider pins.
Slide caliper over the pads. Reinstall slider bolts and torque to 14 ft-lb.
Reinstall wheels, torque lugs to 110 ft-lb.
Pump brake pedal 6–8 times until firm. Top off fluid.
Bed in pads: 8–10 moderate stops from 35 mph, then 2–3 hard stops from 50 mph. Cool down without dragging.
pros: OEM Mopar rotors well-priced and widely stocked
Same caliper architecture as JK — common tools, similar procedure
Powerstop Z36 upgrade is bolt-on, cost-effective for lifted rigs
Job under 2 hours on a familiar truck
cons: Three different rotor packages from the factory — wrong part won't fit
Drilled-and-slotted rotors offer zero benefit and crack faster
Master cylinder sensitive to piston backflow — must open reservoir cap
Rotors warp early on rigs that see water crossings

title: 8HP75 Automatic — Service Intervals and Fluid
tools_required: scan tool with trans temp read or Tazer

parts.name: Mopar 8HP75 filter and pan gasket kit

citations.title: JL 8HP Specific Service Details (JL Wrangler Forums)
Blauparts 8HP50/8HP75 ATF Change Kit
ZF8 50K DIY Procedure (JL Wrangler Forums)

summary: Jeep markets the 8HP75 as "lifetime fill," but ZF — the company that designs it — specifies service every 50,000-80,000 miles, and the gearbox lasts dramatically longer when you actually do it.
description:
The 8HP75 (Mopar code 850RE) is the same ZF-designed eight-speed used in BMW, Ram, and Maserati. It's a remarkable piece of engineering, but the "lifetime fluid" claim is a marketing convenience. ZF's own service literature calls for fluid changes at 50,000-80,000 miles, and shops that rebuild these boxes see the same failure pattern: burnt fluid leads to mechatronic and clutch-pack wear by 120k-150k miles. A $250 fluid service saves a $6,000 rebuild.

The fluid is non-negotiable: Mopar 68218925AB (ZF 8 & 9 speed ATF) or genuine ZF Lifeguard 8. Do not use a "compatible" or "multi-vehicle" ATF. The friction modifiers are specific to the wet clutch packs, and the wrong fluid causes shift flare and clutch glazing within thousands of miles.

The JL pan is metal with a separate bolt-on filter — meaning you can reuse the pan but should replace the filter and gasket every service. Capacity is roughly 9.5 quarts total, but a drain-and-fill only swaps about 5-5.5 quarts (the torque converter holds the rest). For best results, drain-fill twice with 1000 miles between, or run a fluid exchange machine.

The hard part isn't draining — it's filling to the correct level. There is no dipstick. The fill plug doubles as a level check, and the procedure requires the fluid at 86°F-122°F (30°C-50°C), the vehicle level on a lift or all four jack stands, and the trans in Park with the engine running. You need a scan tool (or Tazer) that reads transmission fluid temperature. Below 86°F you under-fill; above 122°F you over-fill. Both kill the box.

If you've never done this and don't have a scan tool that reads trans temp, this is the maintenance task to pay a dealer or independent shop to do. The fluid is cheap; the access is straightforward; the temperature window is what trips people up.
steps: Drive the Jeep until trans is warm (10-15 minutes), then let it cool. Goal is 86°F-122°F at fill time.
Lift all four wheels to level the vehicle. Trans pan rail must be horizontal.
Place a wide drain pan under the trans. Remove the level/fill plug first (8mm Allen) — if you can't get this off, stop, because you can't refill.
Remove pan bolts in a crisscross pattern. Drop the pan slowly — it will be full of fluid.
Remove the bolt-on filter. Note its orientation. Install new filter and new pan gasket. Torque pan bolts to 89 in-lb in crisscross pattern.
From the fill port, pump in fresh fluid until it begins to dribble out (about 5-5.5 quarts).
Start the engine, foot on brake, cycle through P-R-N-D-2-1 holding each gear 3 seconds, return to Park.

With engine running, monitor trans fluid temp via scan tool or Tazer. When temp hits 86°F-122°F, fluid should be at a steady dribble from the fill port. If running fast, pump in more; if dry, you're under-filled.
Install fill plug, torque to 26 ft-lb.
Drive 10 miles checking for leaks and shift quality. Plan a second drain-and-fill at 1,000 miles to refresh the fluid that stayed in the converter.
pros: Extends transmission life by tens of thousands of miles
Pan and filter are accessible without dropping the trans
Mopar fluid is widely available
cons: Requires a scan tool that reads trans fluid temperature
Temperature window for fill is narrow
Two drain-and-fills (or a flush machine) needed to fully refresh fluid
Wrong ATF causes shift flare within thousands of miles

title: eTorque Mild Hybrid — What It Is and What It Isn't

citations.title: What is eTorque and does my Jeep Wrangler have it?
48 volt eTorque battery reliability discussion
Battery issues and How to test 48V eTorque Battery

summary: eTorque is a mild hybrid system that replaces the alternator with a 48V belt-driven motor generator, smooths start-stop, and adds about 90 lb-ft (2.0L turbo) or 130 lb-ft (3.6L V6) of brief assist torque. It is not a plug-in hybrid and it does not let you drive on electric power alone.
description:
If you bought a 2019 or newer JL with the 2.0L turbo, you have eTorque whether you wanted it or not — it's standard on that engine. On the 3.6L Pentastar, eTorque was optional and is identified by the "eTorque" badging or by the second battery under the rear seat. The system has three pieces: a 48V lithium battery pack (under the rear passenger seat), a belt-driven motor generator unit (MGU) where the alternator used to live, and a DC-DC converter that steps 48V down to charge the conventional 12V starter battery.

Here is the part most people miss: the 12V battery still cranks the engine on a cold start, exactly like a non-hybrid Jeep. The MGU only takes over to restart the engine after an auto stop-start shutoff. So when you turn the key first thing in the morning, you're using the same lead-acid battery any JK owner has been using for fifteen years. The 48V battery handles the smooth restart at red lights, captures regen energy on coastdown, and feeds the MGU when it pushes 90 to 130 lb-ft into the crankshaft for the first second or two of acceleration. That brief torque assist is what makes the 2.0L feel quicker than its 270 hp on paper.

Common eTorque problems on JL forums cluster around three things. First, the 12V starter battery still dies — owners often blame eTorque but the 12V is a normal AGM battery that ages on a normal AGM battery timeline (4–6 years in Phoenix heat). Second, the 48V battery occasionally throws codes for hybrid battery coolant sensor or temp sensor faults; dealerships generally replace under warranty. Third, some early 2.0L trucks reported weekly drain even with 14.4V charging — almost always traced to a parasitic draw, not the hybrid system. The 48V battery and related components are covered by an 8 year / 80,000 mile federal hybrid warranty, so most of the expensive failures are not coming out of your wallet.

What eTorque does not do: it does not give you all-electric range, it does not let you bypass the 12V system if it dies, and it does not produce enough sustained torque to matter once you're above idle. Treat it as a smarter alternator that also softens the auto stop-start hand-off.
steps: Identify whether your JL has eTorque by looking for the badge on the rear quarter panel or the second battery box under the rear passenger seat.
If you see a low-battery warning, test the 12V starter battery first — same drill as any AGM battery.
If the 48V hybrid system throws a code (P1A0A, P0A7D, P0AFA, others), document it and take it to a dealer while still under 8/80k warranty.
Do not disconnect or service the orange-shielded 48V cables — high-voltage hybrid wiring requires shop-level safety procedures.
Maintain the 12V battery normally: clean terminals, check resting voltage at 12.6V, replace at 4–6 years.
pros: 48V battery, MGU, and related components covered 8 years / 80,000 miles
Smooths the auto stop-start restart
Adds brief torque assist on takeoff
Improves city MPG by 1–2 mpg
cons: 12V starter battery still dies on a normal schedule, confusing owners
Hybrid components are dealer-service items if out of warranty
Adds weight and complexity vs. a non-eTorque Pentastar
Trail repairs of the high-voltage side are not a DIY job

title: Front Driveshaft Replacement

parts.name: Mopar OEM Rzeppa CV joint repair kit
Tom Wood's JL front 1310 double cardan

citations.title: JK/JL front driveshaft CV failure — JK-Forum
Tom Wood's JL 1310 front shaft

summary: A clunk on throttle tip-in or a vibration that starts after a lift is almost always the front Rzeppa CV joint — the stock shaft is the weak point on every JL, and lifting more than 2.5 inches will kill it faster.
description:
The JL front driveshaft uses a Rzeppa CV joint at the transfer case end and a single u-joint at the axle pinion. The Rzeppa design lets the shaft articulate without the harmonic vibration you get from a u-joint at a steep angle. Stock-height JLs run them for the life of the truck. Lifted JLs eat them, and the failure mode is consistent: a torn boot, grease slung across the underbody, and a clunk every time torque transfers through the joint.

The failure progression is predictable. The Rzeppa boot tears or weeps — sometimes from age, more often from articulation past the joint's design limit. Grease escapes. Dirt and water enter. The bearings inside the joint dry out and start to score. You hear a clunk on acceleration or deceleration, then a vibration that worsens as speed climbs. Catch it at the torn-boot stage and you can clean, regrease, and reboot the joint with a Mopar repair kit around $180. Wait until the clunk shows up and the bearings are already damaged — replace the joint or the whole shaft.

Three replacement paths exist. The OEM Mopar shaft (68272525AC for non-Rubicon JL) at roughly $450 is a direct fit, but it is the same Rzeppa design that just failed. If the Jeep is stock and stays stock, OEM is fine. If you lifted it, replace the failure with something better. A heavy-duty 1310 shaft from Adams Driveshaft or Tom Wood's at $575–$595 uses a double-cardan front joint, which tolerates the steeper operating angle a lifted JL imposes. Heavier-walled tubing means it survives rock hits and torque from larger tires.

Diagnose before you order. Drop the front shaft, hold the CV end, and try to articulate it through its range. A healthy joint moves smoothly and silently. A failed joint clicks, binds, or rolls roughly. Inspect the boot for tears and the centering yoke for play — non-greasable yokes (211544X) and greasable yokes (211355X) both wear. Check the rear u-joint at the pinion end while the shaft is down; replacing one joint without inspecting the other is leaving a job half done.
steps: Park on level ground, chock the rear wheels, and raise the front. Support on jack stands.
Mark the front shaft flange and the pinion yoke with a paint pen so you can reinstall in the same orientation. Phasing matters.
Remove the four 15mm bolts holding the shaft to the front axle pinion yoke.
Remove the four bolts at the transfer case flange (typically 15mm).
Lower the shaft, supporting the weight — it is not heavy but the CV end is fragile if dropped on concrete.
Inspect both joints. If only the CV is bad and the rest of the shaft is sound, install a Mopar repair kit per its instructions. Otherwise install the new shaft.

Bolt the new shaft up with the alignment marks aligned. Torque flange bolts to 22 ft-lbs at the pinion and 22 ft-lbs at the transfer case. Verify clearance from exhaust and skids before lowering the Jeep.
pros: Eliminates the clunk and vibration immediately
Repair kit option keeps the shaft if the bearings are still good
Heavy-duty aftermarket shafts handle lift, 35s, and trail use
Job is 1–2 hours with hand tools
cons: OEM shaft repeats the same failure mode under lift
Aftermarket heavy-duty shafts run $575+
Boots tear from articulation, not just age — lifted Jeeps see more frequent failures
Pinion seal often weeps after a hard CV failure and may need replacement too

title: Rear Locker Options — Dana 35 and Dana 44

parts.name: ARB Air Locker RD100 — Dana 35 (JL Sport/Sahara)
ARB Air Locker RD156 — Dana 44 (JL Rubicon)

citations.title: ARB Air Locker Product Overview
Eaton ELocker Installation and Specs
Detroit Truetrac Dana 35 Product Page

summary: A rear locker changes the JL's off-road capability more dramatically than almost any other single upgrade — but your rear axle (Dana 35 vs Dana 44) determines which lockers are available, and those axle differences also determine whether a locker is the right investment or whether an axle upgrade should come first.
description:
The axle situation on the JL is the critical starting context. JL Sport and Sport S models come with a Dana 35 rear axle — a solid, competent axle for street and mild trail use, but lighter-duty than the Dana 44. The Sahara also ships with the Dana 35 in most configurations. The Rubicon (and the Rubicon 392) gets the Dana 44, which is the significantly stronger choice for technical trail use. If you're on a Sport or Sahara and considering a locker, you need to decide whether you're locking a Dana 35 long-term or upgrading to a Dana 44 carrier down the road — because the lockers are not interchangeable.

For the Dana 35 (Sport/Sahara), the two realistic choices are the ARB Air Locker ($799) or the Detroit Truetrac ($449). The Truetrac is not technically a locker — it's a helical gear limited-slip differential that provides significant bias toward the wheel with traction under load, but does not achieve full lock. For mild-to-moderate trail use on a rig that sees pavement regularly, the Truetrac is the right choice: it's transparent on-road, requires no compressor or electrical system, and the $449 price point is accessible. For genuine rock crawling where complete drive wheel lock is required, the Truetrac falls short.

The ARB Air Locker for the Dana 35 ($799) delivers full lock on demand. ARB's air locker engages via an onboard air compressor (required separately — budget $150–$300 for a basic unit) and disengages cleanly when the air is released. The on-road behavior when unlocked is stock-equivalent. The ARB is the correct choice for a Dana 35 build that sees sustained technical terrain. Just be realistic: a Dana 35 with a locker will eventually meet a trail that exceeds the axle's shaft strength. Know your terrain.

For the Dana 44 (Rubicon), both the ARB Air Locker ($849) and Eaton ELocker ($649) are full-lock solutions with different engagement mechanisms. The ARB requires a compressor; the Eaton ELocker engages electrically via a dash switch. The ELocker is the value choice for a Rubicon build — $200 less than the ARB, no compressor required, reliable engagement, and the electrical install is cleaner. The ARB's advantage is faster engagement response and the ability to share the compressor with ARB lockers front and rear, plus tire inflation duties.

Rubicon owners note: the factory Selec-Trac II transfer case includes an electronic rear locker. If your Rubicon already has the factory locker, evaluate whether an aftermarket locker adds meaningful capability before spending $649–$849.
steps: Drain the differential fluid before any disassembly.
Support the rear axle on jack stands and remove both rear wheels.
Remove the rear brake drums or caliper/rotor assemblies (depending on trim) and disconnect the axle shafts.
Mark the bearing caps before removal — they are directional and must return to the same position.
Remove the carrier bearing caps and extract the ring gear/carrier assembly.
Transfer the ring gear to the locker carrier per manufacturer instructions. New ring gear bolts should be used — old bolts stretch and should not be reused.

Set ring gear backlash and bearing preload per manufacturer specs using a dial indicator. This step requires patience and is the most critical part of the install — incorrect backlash causes noise, premature wear, or failure.
For ARB: route air lines through the axle housing per the included instructions before reinstalling carrier.
Reinstall carrier, torque bearing caps to spec.
Reconnect axle shafts, reinstall brakes, reinstall wheels.
For ARB: mount the air compressor, route air lines to the cab switch per install instructions.
For Eaton ELocker: route electrical harness to the cab switch location per install instructions.
Refill differential with gear oil per manufacturer's fluid spec — some lockers require specific viscosity.
Test locker engagement off the vehicle before returning to trail. Drive slowly, confirm engagement and disengagement.
pros: A rear locker delivers the most direct off-road capability gain of any single JL upgrade — full traction to both rear wheels in a bind
ARB Air Locker is the gold standard for on-demand, full-lock engagement with stock-equivalent on-road behavior
Eaton ELocker delivers full lock at lower cost than ARB with no compressor requirement
Detroit Truetrac is the right answer for a Dana 35 on a mild-trail rig that sees significant pavement
ARB compressor (required for air locker) doubles as a trail inflation tool — functional overlap
cons: Dana 35 (Sport/Sahara) is a lighter-duty axle than the Dana 44 — a locker increases the load on the axle shafts, which are already the weak point; know your terrain limits
ARB Air Locker installation requires a compressor and plumbing, adding cost and complexity beyond the locker itself
Setting ring gear backlash correctly requires a dial indicator and specific knowledge; this is not a beginner install
Incorrect carrier bearing preload will cause differential noise within the first few hundred miles — don't skip the setup spec steps
Eaton ELocker is not available for the Dana 35 — Sport/Sahara owners are limited to ARB or Truetrac
Rubicon's factory electronic rear locker may make an aftermarket locker redundant — evaluate factory capability before purchasing

title: Re-Gearing the JL — 4.56 and 4.88 Ratio Selection

parts.name: Yukon Gear Ring and Pinion 4.88 — Dana 35 Rear
Yukon Gear Ring and Pinion 4.88 — Dana 44 Rear
Yukon Gear Ring and Pinion 4.88 — Dana 30 Front
Yukon Gear Master Overhaul Kit — Dana 44

citations.title: Yukon Gear JL Wrangler Ring and Pinion Sets
Ring and Pinion Ratio Selection Guide — Quadratec
Dana 35 vs Dana 44 Comparison Guide

summary: The stock gear ratios on most JL trims were sized for street-biased tires — if you've moved to 35s or 37s and haven't regeared, you're working the drivetrain harder than it was designed for and leaving significant trail capability on the table.
description:
The math behind regearing is straightforward. Your engine makes peak torque in a specific RPM range. Larger tires rotate more slowly per mile, which effectively changes your final drive ratio and moves your RPM operating point down out of that optimal range. The result: sluggish acceleration, transmission hunting on grades, and a crawl ratio that feels inadequate on steep technical terrain. Regearing restores the RPM relationship to a range the drivetrain was designed to operate in.

JL gear ratio context by trim:
- **Sahara:** Stock 3.45. With 35s, move to 4.56. With 37s, move to 4.88.
- **Sport/Sport S:** Stock 3.73. With 35s, 4.10 is acceptable; 4.56 is better. With 37s, 4.88.
- **Rubicon:** Stock 4.10. With 35s, 4.10 is workable; 4.56 improves trail performance meaningfully. With 37s, 4.56 at minimum; 4.88 for serious rock builds.

The Sahara with 3.45 gears and 37s is the worst-case scenario — the highway RPM drop is noticeable, low-speed trail control is compromised, and the transmission is working in a range it wasn't mapped for. This is not a "it runs, just a bit slow" situation; it's a configuration that accelerates powertrain wear. Regear before running 37s on a Sahara.

**Front and rear must be regeared together.** Running mismatched ratios front to rear on a part-time 4WD system causes severe binding and drivetrain damage when 4WD is engaged. This is not optional.

Yukon Gear is the benchmark brand for JL ring and pinion sets. Their steel quality is consistent, the manufacturing tolerances are tight (which simplifies setup), and they support both Dana 30/35 (Sport/Sahara) and Dana 44 (Rubicon) fitments. The master overhaul kit ($249) includes all bearings, races, seals, shims, and hardware needed to complete the job — don't attempt to reuse factory bearings on a regear.

**Labor consideration:** Setting up ring and pinion gears correctly is one of the most skill-dependent jobs in the drivetrain world. Incorrect backlash or bearing preload will cause gear noise, premature wear, or catastrophic failure within 10,000 miles. If you haven't done it before, the first regear should be done at a reputable 4WD shop — watch, learn, then DIY the second axle.
steps: Drain differential fluid from both axles before disassembly.
Front axle: support axle, remove wheels, disconnect front driveshaft, remove axle shafts.
Remove front diff cover, mark bearing cap positions before removal.
Extract carrier/ring gear assembly, remove pinion.
Press old pinion and carrier bearings off using a bearing puller or press.
Install new pinion bearings on new pinion. Set pinion depth using shim stack (this requires a dial indicator and pattern checking — follow Yukon's instructions precisely).
Install pinion, set pinion bearing preload to manufacturer spec using an inch-pound torque wrench.
Transfer ring gear to carrier (or install new carrier if upgrading). Install new ring gear bolts — do not reuse old bolts.
Set carrier bearing preload and ring gear backlash to spec. Check gear mesh contact pattern with gear marking compound — the pattern must be centered before final assembly.
Install diff cover with new gasket, torque to spec.
Repeat procedure for rear axle (Dana 35 or Dana 44 depending on trim).
Fill both differentials with correct gear oil per manufacturer spec (some ring and pinion installs require specific break-in fluid — follow Yukon's recommendation).
Drive gently for the first 500 miles. Avoid sustained high-speed runs during break-in. Change break-in fluid at 500 miles.
pros: Restores factory RPM operating range after tire size increase — the single most important drivetrain step for builds running 35s or 37s
Dramatically improves trail crawl ratio, low-speed control, and pull-away performance
4.88 gears on a Sahara with 37s transforms a sluggish street-and-parking-lot Jeep into a capable trail rig
Yukon Gear's quality and documentation are the best in the class for JL fitments
Regear done alongside a locker install saves a second teardown — plan both jobs together when possible
cons: Difficulty 5 — incorrect gear mesh setup causes noise and failure; this is the most technically demanding job on a Jeep
Both axles must be done simultaneously, doubling the parts cost
Parts alone run $650–$800 (front + rear gear sets plus master kit); shop labor adds $1,200–$1,600 for the pair, making total installed cost $2,000–$2,400
Break-in period requires restraint — spirited driving in the first 500 miles risks premature gear wear
Dana 35 (Sport/Sahara rear) has a smaller ring gear and lighter shafts — regearing it to 4.88 doesn't change the fact that it's a lighter-duty axle
The Rubicon 392 has a different rear axle (Dana 44 AdvanTEK) with different gear selection — verify exact axle spec before purchasing gears

title: Engine Air Filter Replacement — 3.6L

citations.title: Mopar 68257030AA Air Filter — Quadratec
Jeep Air Filter Change Wrangler JL 3.6L — CheaperJeeperTV

summary: Pop four clips, swap the filter, done. The JL 3.6L Pentastar uses Mopar 68257030AA — replace it every 30,000 miles or sooner if you run dusty trails.
description:
The JL's airbox sits at the front passenger corner of the engine bay with four metal spring clips holding the lid down. No tools required for a stock replacement — though a flathead screwdriver helps pry the clips if they've never been opened. The whole job runs about 10 minutes and the OEM Mopar filter is $20–25 from any dealer or Quadratec. Aftermarket drop-ins from K&N or aFe are double the price; the genuine Mopar paper element flows plenty for a stock 3.6L and traps finer dust than oiled cotton-gauze filters.

Open the hood and look at the front passenger side. The airbox is the big black plastic shroud with the intake snorkel running up to the cowl. Run a finger along the seam between the lid and the lower box — you'll feel the four spring clips, two front and two rear. Pop each clip outward with your thumb or a screwdriver tip. Lift the lid up and toward the front of the Jeep; the intake tube on the back stays connected, the lid just hinges.

The old filter pulls straight up. Note its orientation — the rubber seal sits on top, the pleats face down. Wipe out any leaves or dirt in the lower airbox with a shop rag before dropping the new filter in. Don't blow it out with compressed air unless you've removed the MAF sensor tube — debris can fire backward through the system and contaminate the mass airflow sensor.

Drop the new filter in with the seal facing up and pleats facing down. Press the lid back down — make sure the front edge tucks under its lip — and snap the four clips back into place. Pull on the lid once to confirm it's seated. If you feel air whistle through the seal when the engine runs, the lid isn't fully clipped.

Most JL owners running pavement-only can stretch this to 40,000 miles. Phoenix dust, Moab trips, or sand washes drop the interval to 15,000–20,000. Hold the old filter up to a shop light; if you can't see light through it, it's overdue.
steps: Open the hood and locate the airbox at the front passenger corner.
Pop the four spring clips on the airbox lid (thumb or flathead screwdriver).
Lift the lid up and toward the front; the intake tube stays connected.
Lift the old filter straight up out of the box.
Wipe out any debris in the lower airbox with a rag — do not use compressed air.
Set the new filter in with seal facing up, pleats facing down.
Tuck the front edge of the lid under its lip and press the lid down.
Snap all four spring clips back into place.
Tug the lid to confirm it's seated, close the hood.
pros: 10-minute job with no tools required
OEM Mopar filter is $20–25 and fits perfectly
No risk of over-oiling and contaminating the MAF (a known issue with some oiled cotton filters)
cons: Performance gains from aftermarket filters are mostly marketing on a stock 3.6L
Spring clips can pinch fingers if they snap shut on you
Hot-rodded JLs running tunes may still want a full intake system, not just a drop-in

title: Battery Replacement — Start-Stop and eTorque Systems

citations.title: JL Wrangler Forums — Main and Aux Battery Size
2021 3.6 eTorque OEM Battery Specs
Wrangler Forum — Auxiliary Battery AGM Discussion

summary: The JL uses an AGM H7 main battery — replace it with AGM, not a flooded lead-acid, or the start-stop system will fail and the BCM will log faults.
description:
The 2018+ Wrangler JL ships with an AGM H7 (BCI group 94R) main battery — typically 80 Ah and 850 CCA. eTorque trims (2.0L turbo and 3.6L with the 48V mild hybrid) add a small 12V AUX14 auxiliary AGM battery rated around 200 CCA, plus the separate 48V lithium-ion pack that handles the mild hybrid functions. The 48V pack carries an 8-year warranty and is not a DIY part. The auxiliary 12V AGM and the main H7, however, are both owner-serviceable.

Use AGM only. The JL's body control module is configured for AGM charging voltage and current profiles. Drop in a flooded lead-acid battery and the BCM will overcharge it on highway runs and undercharge it during ESS stop events, which kills the battery in months and throws "Service Stop/Start System" warnings. Quality H7 AGM options include Mopar OEM (Interstate MTX-94R/H7), Odyssey AGM94R, Optima YELLOWTOP DH7, and the OEM eTorque part 56029720AA. Expect to pay $250–$350 for a quality H7 AGM.

The auxiliary battery on start-stop and eTorque trims lives on the passenger side firewall under a small cover. It powers electronics during the ESS engine-off pause so cabin power, infotainment, and HVAC don't drop out. When it fails, ESS stops working and you'll see a service message — but the truck still runs fine on the main battery alone. Replacement AUX14 batteries run $90–$140.

After replacing either battery, the BCM needs to register the new battery so it can manage charging correctly. On non-eTorque JLs the system usually self-relearns within a few drive cycles. On eTorque trims, a Mopar dealer or aftermarket scan tool (Topdon, Autel, wiTECH) is recommended to perform a battery registration. Without registration, the alternator may not properly charge the new battery, shortening its life by half.
steps: Park on level ground and turn off all accessories. Open the driver door so the BCM stays awake briefly.
Optional: plug a memory saver into the OBD-II port to preserve radio presets and adaptive transmission learning.
Open the hood. Loosen the 10mm negative (black) terminal clamp on the main battery first. Tuck the cable aside.
Loosen the 10mm positive (red) terminal clamp and remove the plastic cover. Tuck the cable aside.
Remove the 13mm battery hold-down bracket bolt at the front base of the battery.
Lift the battery straight up — it weighs roughly 50 pounds.
Clean the tray and terminals with a battery brush. Inspect for corrosion or moisture damage.
Set the new AGM battery in place with terminals matching the original orientation.
Reinstall the hold-down bracket and torque the 13mm bolt snug — do not overtighten.
Connect the positive terminal first, then the negative. Tighten the 10mm clamps until snug.
For eTorque or start-stop trims, perform a battery registration with a scan tool that supports BCM coding.
For the auxiliary battery: open the passenger-side firewall cover, disconnect the small terminals (10mm), remove the strap, and swap. Reverse to install.
pros: 30–60 minute job in the driveway
$250 DIY vs. $500+ at the dealer
Restores start-stop function and clears service messages
AGM batteries handle deep-cycle abuse better than flooded
cons: Battery registration may require a scan tool on eTorque trims
AGM costs roughly 2x a flooded H7
The 48V lithium pack on eTorque is dealer-only
AUX14 auxiliary battery is buried behind a firewall cover

title: Differential Fluid Change — Dana 44 Front and Rear

citations.title: Motobilt — Jeep Wrangler Differential Fluid Capacity Chart
JL Wrangler Forums — Rubicon Rear Differential Gear Oil Capacity Surprise
JL Wrangler Forums — Differential Fluid Discussion

summary: The JL Dana 44 axles take less fluid than the JK they replaced — about 1.5 quarts per axle — and Mopar specifies 75W-85 GL-5 gear oil, with 4 oz of friction modifier added to any Trac-Lok differential.
description:
The JL inherited the Dana 44 designation but the axles themselves are new — they're called AdvanTEK and they hold noticeably less fluid than the JK Dana 44. Plan on 1.4 to 1.6 quarts per axle (front and rear), not the 2.3 quarts you'd put in a JK. Overfilling is a real risk because the fill plug is positioned higher than the actual fill line on some axle covers — fluid coming out of the hole doesn't always mean the diff is full to spec. Trust the manual capacity and measure what goes in.

Mopar's recommended fluid is 75W-85 GL-5 hypoid gear oil (part #68218057AA). The owner's manual for some JL configurations also lists 75W-140 for severe trailer-towing use. For 99% of owners running street and trail, 75W-85 is correct. Any name-brand GL-5 in that viscosity works — Mobil 1 Synthetic 75W-90 is a common and acceptable substitute, despite being a half-step heavier.

Trac-Lok limited-slip rear axles (standard on Sahara, optional on Sport S) require friction modifier. The Mopar additive is part #04318060AC, 4 ounces per axle. Without it, the clutches will chatter on slow corners — you'll hear it as a series of clunks from the rear end when turning. Lockers (Rubicon front and rear) do not need friction modifier.

The first fluid change matters most. Factory fill carries break-in metal from the ring and pinion. Mopar's service interval is 67,500 miles for normal use, 30,000 for severe service — but pulling the cover at 5,000–7,500 miles after delivery and replacing the fluid is cheap insurance. After the first change, every 30,000 miles is reasonable; sooner if you submerge the axles or wheel in mud often.

There is no drain plug on the AdvanTEK covers — you remove the cover to drain. That makes this a bigger job than it sounds, because you'll need to clean the cover, the magnet, and the housing mating surface, then re-seal with RTV. Bolts are 13mm, torque to 30 ft-lb in a cross pattern. Wait at least an hour for the RTV to skin before adding fluid.
steps: Park on level ground. Warm the axles by driving a few miles — warm fluid drains cleaner.
Place a wide drain pan under the diff cover. Remove the fill plug FIRST (1/2" ratchet drive). If it won't break loose, stop — you don't want to drain a diff you can't refill.
Crack the bottom cover bolts, then loosen the upper bolts. Leave the top two snug and let the cover hang open at the bottom to drain.
Once drained, remove all bolts and pull the cover. Inspect the magnet — fine fuzz is normal, chunks or chips are not.
Clean the cover, magnet, and housing mating surface with brake cleaner. Both surfaces must be bare metal and dry.
Apply a 1/8" bead of Ultra Black RTV around the cover, encircling each bolt hole. Install cover and torque bolts to 30 ft-lb in a cross pattern.
Wait one hour for RTV to set.
Use a fluid pump to add 1.5 quarts of 75W-85 GL-5 through the fill hole. Add 4 oz friction modifier first if Trac-Lok.
Reinstall fill plug, torque to 25 ft-lb. Clean any drips.
pros: Cheap insurance against ring-and-pinion wear
Catches early bearing failure (metal on magnet)
30,000-mile interval is reasonable for a trail-driven JL
Lockers don't need friction modifier — simpler than older Trac-Lok-only platforms
cons: No drain plug — full cover removal required
RTV cure time blocks the job for an hour
Fill plug position can fool you into overfilling — measure what goes in
Trac-Lok chatter is the symptom of missed friction modifier, and the fix is another fluid change

title: Oil Change — Pentastar 3.6L and eTorque

parts.name: 0W-20 full synthetic oil (5–6 quarts depending on year)

citations.title: 2018+ JL Wrangler owner's manual — 3.6L oil spec 0W-20
JL 3.6L Pentastar oil capacity (5 qt non-eTorque, 5.5 qt eTorque)
Pentastar cartridge filter housing torque 25 Nm

summary: The JL Pentastar moved from 5W-20 (JK) to 0W-20 full synthetic. Use a cartridge filter — there's no spin-on. Drain plug torques to 20 ft-lb, filter cap to 18 ft-lb. eTorque models hold half a quart more oil than non-eTorque.
description:
The 3.6L Pentastar in the JL is the same basic engine that was in the late JK, but FCA changed the oil spec from 5W-20 to 0W-20 for fuel economy. Either viscosity will run the engine; the 0W-20 reduces cold-start friction and helps the start-stop and eTorque systems behave smoothly. Use what the manual calls for and the OBD-II long-term fuel trims will stay where they should.

**Capacity.** 5.0 quarts on non-eTorque (2018+) and 5.5 quarts on eTorque mild-hybrid models with filter change. Always verify with the dipstick — overfilling causes the same intake-valve-coking issue the Pentastar is already prone to from direct injection.

**Filter.** Cartridge type, same plastic housing on top of the engine as the JK. Mopar 68191349AC is the OEM part. The plastic cap cracks under abuse — a 76mm 14-flute cap socket is the only correct tool. If a previous shop used channel locks and the cap is gouged, replace it before it splits in service (Mopar 68191344AB, ~$30).

**eTorque caveat.** eTorque adds a 48V belt-driven starter/generator (BSG) on the front of the engine. It doesn't change the oil change procedure, but it does mean the engine may auto-start during the change if you don't disconnect the 48V battery or follow the service mode procedure (turn ignition to RUN, then to OFF, then immediately disconnect 12V negative). Don't skip this on eTorque trucks.
steps: Run engine 2–3 minutes to thin the oil. Shut off.
**eTorque only:** Cycle key to RUN then OFF, then immediately disconnect 12V negative terminal. This prevents auto-start during the change.
Pull the engine cover (friction fit).
Loosen the filter cap one turn to let oil drain into the housing before pulling the drain plug.
Position drain pan under oil pan. Remove 13mm drain plug. Drain 5+ minutes.
Remove filter cap completely. Lift out old cartridge. Wipe housing.
Replace cap O-ring. Lubricate new O-ring with fresh oil. Snap new cartridge into cap. Reinstall, torque to 25 Nm (18 ft-lb).
Install drain plug with new crush washer. Torque to 20 ft-lb.
Add 5 qt (non-eTorque) or 5.5 qt (eTorque) of 0W-20 full synthetic through the cap.
Reconnect 12V if disconnected. Start engine; verify oil pressure light goes out within 3 seconds.
Wait 5 minutes, check dipstick. Top off as needed — do not overfill.
pros: Top-mount filter, no crawling
30–60 minute job
Common 0W-20 synthetic at any parts store
Same procedure regardless of door count or transmission
cons: Plastic filter cap requires care
eTorque adds a battery-disconnect step
Wrong viscosity (especially old 5W-30 inventory) will trigger fuel trim drift on long-term monitors
Pentastar still loves to coke intake valves — frequent oil changes help but don't solve it

title: Spark Plug Replacement — 3.6L Pentastar

citations.title: iFixit — Spark plug replacement, 2018-2024 JL 3.6L
WAYALIFE JL torque specs reference
JLwranglerforums — spark plug change on 3.6 Pentastar

summary: Replace all six iridium plugs every 100,000 miles. Torque to 13 ft-lb (17.5 N·m) — the 12mm Pentastar plugs strip if you over-tighten. Plan on an hour in the driveway.
description:
The 3.6L Pentastar in the JL uses 12mm spark plugs — smaller than the 14mm plugs in older Jeep engines. That matters for two reasons. First, the spark plug socket is 5/8" (16mm), not the 13/16" that fits the 4.0L. Second, the thinner shell strips its threads at much lower torque, so a regular click-type torque wrench set to "feel" is not good enough. Use a wrench that reads in inch-pounds or one that goes down to single-digit foot-pounds.

NGK ILKAR7L11 is the direct factory equivalent and runs about $55 for a set of six. Mopar's branded plug is the same NGK part with a Chrysler box and a markup. There is no benefit to going up a heat range or to a one-step-colder plug on a stock motor — the OEM iridium plugs are correct for stock and lightly modified Pentastars. Skip the anti-seize; NGK explicitly says not to use it on iridium plugs, and the plated threads do not need it.

Access on the JL is straightforward. The coil packs sit on top of each cylinder, held by a single 10mm bolt. Remove the bolt, twist the coil to break the rubber boot seal, lift it off, and you are looking at the plug well. Use a 6-inch extension and the 5/8" plug socket. The plug well is deep — a magnetic or rubber-insert socket keeps the old plug from dropping into the head when you back it out.

Reinstall each new plug by hand first to confirm thread engagement — never start a plug with a ratchet. Torque to 13 ft-lb (17.5 N·m). A dab of dielectric grease inside the coil boot helps it pull off cleanly the next time. Reinstall the coil with the 10mm bolt, repeat for the remaining five cylinders. Total job time is about an hour the first time, 30 minutes after that.

Symptoms that mean it is time: rough idle at startup, misfire code (P0301–P0306), or a noticeable loss of low-end response. Most JLs make it to the 100,000-mile interval cleanly. Track-driven or extreme cold-climate Jeeps benefit from inspecting at 75,000.
steps: Cold engine. Disconnect the negative battery cable (10mm).
Remove the engine cover (pulls straight up off four rubber grommets).
Pick a coil pack. Remove the 10mm coil hold-down bolt.
Unclip the coil electrical connector. Twist and lift the coil out.
Drop the 5/8" plug socket on a 6-inch extension into the well. Back the plug out counterclockwise.
Verify the gap on the new plug (factory pre-gap is correct — do not regap iridium).
Hand-thread the new plug. Then torque to 13 ft-lb.
Apply dielectric grease inside the coil boot. Reinstall coil, bolt, and connector.
Repeat for the remaining five cylinders.
Reinstall engine cover, reconnect battery, start, listen for smooth idle.
pros: 100,000-mile interval — set-and-forget maintenance
Job runs about $60 in parts vs. $200+ at a shop
Restores throttle response and cold-start smoothness
Direct access — no manifold removal needed
cons: 12mm plugs strip easily if you over-torque
Coil boots can tear if the rubber has aged
Plug socket must be the deep 5/8" type with a retainer
Skipping torque spec is the #1 way to crack a coil

title: Transfer Case Fluid Change — MPT/FCA 8HP Considerations

citations.title: Trail Wrangler — Jeep JL Transfer Case fluid change
JL Wrangler Forums — MP3022C fluid change

summary: Use Mopar ATF+4 (or an MS-9602-rated multi-vehicle ATF) in every JL transfer case — MP3022 on Rubicon, NV241 on Sport/Sahara, MP1522 on 4xe — and budget 1.7 to 2.0 quarts for the refill.
description:
The JL's transfer case requires ATF, not gear oil — this trips up owners coming from XJ or TJ platforms where the t-case ran the same 75W-90 as the axles. The Mopar spec is MS-9602, which is the same fluid family as ATF+4. Any name-brand ATF+4 or a multi-vehicle ATF that lists MS-9602 compatibility (Valvoline MaxLife, Castrol Transmax) will hold up. Mopar's official position is ATF+4 only. The aftermarket position is that MS-9602-compatible fluids work fine; pick your comfort level.

Capacity depends on the case. The MP3022 (Rubicon two-speed with 4LO) shows around 1.7–1.85 quarts on a proper drain and refill. The NV241 on Sport/Sahara is similar. The MP1522 found on 4xe takes about 2.0 quarts. Service manuals occasionally underreport — buy two quarts and bring a third if you have it.

Both plugs use a 3/8" square drive or a 13mm hex on most years — pop them open before you crawl under to verify.
