Open the fill plug first; same rule as a diff — if you can't open the fill, don't drain. Position a low-profile pan under the case, open the drain plug, let it run. Inspect what comes out. ATF should look reddish; if it's brown or smells burnt, the case has been working hard and you may want to plan a second drain in 5,000 miles to flush remaining contamination.

Reinstall the drain plug at 20 ft-lbs. Pump new ATF into the fill hole until it overflows — that's the level, do not try to add more. Reinstall the fill plug at 20 ft-lbs. Run the rig through the 2H/4H/N/4L positions a few times in a parking lot to circulate the new fluid through the chain.
steps: Drive the rig 10 minutes to warm the fluid.
Park level, set the parking brake, chock front tires.
Locate the transfer case behind the transmission, between the front and rear driveshafts.
Loosen the fill plug first to verify it opens.
Place a drain pan, open the drain plug, let drain fully.
Inspect drained fluid color and smell.
Reinstall drain plug at 20 ft-lbs with fresh crush washer if equipped.
Pump fresh ATF+4 (or MS-9602 ATF) into the fill hole until it overflows.
Reinstall the fill plug at 20 ft-lbs.
Cycle through 2H/4H/4L positions to circulate.
pros: One of the cheapest scheduled-service items on a JL
Catches water intrusion that ruins chain and bearings
1 hour with the rig on the ground (no lift required)
Fluid is the same as transmission and power steering — easy to stock
cons: Mopar restricts the official spec to ATF+4, limiting bulk purchase options
Service position is awkward without ramps
Two stripped plug heads (square-drive 3/8) are common — chase down a fresh tool if yours is rounded

title: Rooftop Tent and Awning Setup for the JL

parts.name: ARB Simpson III Hardshell Rooftop Tent
CVT Mt. Rainier Hard Shell Rooftop Tent

citations.title: iKamper Skycamp Mini Product Page
ARB Simpson III Tent Overview
Tepui by Thule Autana Softshell Tent

summary: The JL Wrangler's factory roof is rated at 165 lbs static load — that's not the tent's weight limit, it's the roof's structural limit, and the right rack and mounting setup is what keeps you sleeping soundly instead of lying under rubble.
description:
The 165 lbs static / 150 lbs dynamic rating is the number that governs your tent and rack choices on the JL. Static load is the tent plus two adults lying in it, measured when the vehicle is stationary. Dynamic load is everything minus roughly 10–15%, accounting for driving-induced forces. Most hardshell tents fall between 100–140 lbs — that's the tent shell, the platform, and the mattress. Two adults in the 150–200 lb combined range push the dynamic load limit at highway speeds. The solution is not to avoid the tent — it's to use a proper rack system designed for the JL's roof structure, which distributes that load across multiple points rather than concentrating it on the factory cross-bar mounts.

**Rack requirement:** The factory JL roof rails are not sufficient for a rooftop tent without additional support. You need a JL-specific roof rack or cross-bar system from Rhino-Rack, Yakima, or Thule — all of which offer JL-specific fitments that clamp to the factory tracks without drilling. These racks spread the load across the roof structure rather than loading the factory T-slots directly. Budget $300–$600 for a quality rack system before adding the tent.

The iKamper Skycamp Mini 2.0 at $2,499 is the premium choice and for good reason. The Mini's clamshell hardshell design opens in 20 seconds and provides a sleeping platform for two adults in a compact footprint that's shorter than most full-size RTTs. The 3.5" high-density foam mattress is genuinely comfortable, and the tent folds down to a low-profile 7" height on the roof. The Mini also comes in under 110 lbs, which is the most favorable weight-to-roof-rating ratio of the premium options.

The ARB Simpson III at $1,699 is the value hardshell choice with proven trail credibility. ARB builds equipment for serious expeditions and the Simpson III's seam quality and zipper durability reflect that — it's spec'd for sustained outback use, not weekend glamping. At 94 lbs, it's the lightest hardshell on this list, which matters on a JL.

The CVT Mt. Rainier at $1,799 offers a slightly larger sleep platform than the ARB at a competitive price. CVT is a Utah-based brand with a strong reputation in the overlanding community, and their quality control is consistent. The Mt. Rainier's 4" mattress is notably comfortable compared to thinner options.

The Tepui Autana at $1,099 is the softshell entry — lower cost, lighter when folded (62 lbs), but requires a longer setup time (2–5 minutes) and the nylon shell accumulates condensation in ways hardshell designs don't. The Autana is a functional choice for seasonal fair-weather use or builds where budget is a hard constraint.

The ARB 2500 Awning at $299 is the single highest-value-per-dollar addition to an overlanding JL — a shaded cooking and relaxing area deployed in 60 seconds. The 8.2' x 8.2' footprint provides genuine shade. It mounts to the roof rack side rail and is compatible with the same racks as the tent options above.
steps: Install the roof rack system first. Follow the JL-specific instructions for your rack brand (Rhino-Rack, Yakima, or Thule). Confirm the rack is torqued to the mounting specs — under-torqued racks shift under tent load.
Position the tent on the rack. Most RTTs mount with 4 or 6 bolts through the tent's base platform into the rack's cross bars. Measure the mounting bolt pattern before positioning.
With a helper, lift the tent assembly onto the rack. Hardshell tents weigh 90–120 lbs — this is a two-person job. Use a step ladder or work on a level surface.
Insert mounting hardware through the base platform and into the rack T-slot nuts or cross-bar channel. Start all bolts finger-tight before torquing.
Confirm the tent is centered and square on the roof before final torquing. Off-center tent placement affects roof load distribution.
Torque mounting hardware to the tent manufacturer's spec (typically 35–50 ft-lb on the main mount bolts).
Open the tent fully and confirm the hinge mechanism operates correctly and the ladder deploys and locks.
For the ARB awning: mount the awning bracket to the side of the rack rail, route the awning roll correctly, and test deployment before the first camp.
Drive 50 miles on highway and recheck all mounting torque before first overnight use.
pros: Hardshell designs (iKamper, ARB, CVT) set up in under 60 seconds — faster than a ground tent
iKamper Skycamp Mini's 110 lb weight is the most favorable for JL roof load ratings
ARB's expedition-grade construction is field-proven on vehicles that cross the Australian outback
The ARB awning at $299 delivers outsized utility relative to cost — shade and wind break for cooking, eating, and gear organization
RTT elevation keeps you off cold or wet ground and away from ground-level wildlife concerns
cons: Factory JL roof rails require a supplementary rack system before any RTT can be safely mounted — add $300–$600 to tent cost
165 lb static roof limit requires careful attention to tent weight plus occupant weight — understand the rating before purchasing a heavy tent
Hardshell tents add significant aerodynamic drag and wind noise at highway speed — fuel economy drops noticeably
RTT setup requires highway stops to open/close the tent for each camp — not suited to itineraries with multiple camp moves per day
Softshell (Tepui) condensation management requires ventilation habit changes vs sleeping inside a hardshell
The iKamper Skycamp Mini is premium-priced — if cost is a primary constraint, the ARB Simpson III delivers the core functionality at $800 less

title: Recovery Gear Starter Kit for the JL

parts.name: Bubba Rope 20' Gator-Jaw Synthetic Kinetic Recovery Rope
Rhino USA Heavy Duty 3/4" D-Ring Shackles (pair)

citations.title: ARB Recovery Kit RK11B Overview
Bubba Rope Kinetic vs Static Strap Guide
Maxtrax MKII Traction Board Instructions

summary: Before you go anywhere technical in a JL, you need a recovery kit — not because the Wrangler gets stuck often, but because when it does, the tools to get yourself out should be on the rig, not at home.
description:
Recovery gear is split into two functional categories: things that pull you out (straps, shackles, snatch blocks) and things that get you unstuck without needing another vehicle (traction boards, traction mats, a high-lift jack). A complete starter kit covers both. You don't need every item on day one, but you should understand what each does before you need it.

The ARB Recovery Kit ($499) is the fastest way to check off most of the list at once. The RK11B includes a kinetic recovery strap, tree saver strap, snatch block, shackles, and a recovery damper — all in a gear bag. ARB's quality control on strap strength ratings is consistent, and the kit is assembled by people who understand recovery rigging rather than marketing. The $499 price is higher than sourcing individual budget parts, but you're getting components with verified strength ratings and a known source.

If you're building your kit piece by piece, the Bubba Rope Gator-Jaw at $119 is the correct kinetic strap choice. Kinetic ropes stretch under load and use stored elastic energy to help break a vehicle free — they're dramatically more effective than static tow straps for a stuck vehicle and create less violent loading on both vehicles in the recovery. The 20' length is appropriate for most JL-to-JL or JL-to-recovery-vehicle distances. Do not substitute a static tow strap for a kinetic rope on a hard pull.

Maxtrax MKII traction boards ($349/pair) are for self-recovery without another vehicle. The ridged plastic boards wedge under a spinning tire and give it something to grip. They work on sand, mud, and loose terrain. The MKII design is the current iteration — the ribs are sized to work with 32"–37" tires. At $349, the pair is an investment, but cheaper alternatives sacrifice the ridge geometry that makes MKII effective. Budget alternatives at $80–$120/pair exist, but the recovery rate drops.

The Factor 55 FlatLink ($65) is for winch-equipped JLs. It replaces the hook at the end of your winch rope with a flat, low-profile shackle mount that's compatible with soft shackles and eliminates the dangerous projectile risk of a steel hook in a failed recovery. If you have a winch, the FlatLink should be on the rig.
steps: Identify the storage location in your JL for the recovery kit — most JL builds use a dedicated cargo organizer, a Pelican case, or a soft bag stored in the cargo area behind the rear seat.
Inspect all items in the ARB kit before the first trail day — verify strap condition, shackle ratings, and snatch block operation.

For traction boards: practice insertion and extraction before you need them in a real situation. The correct technique is to push them under the spinning tire perpendicular to the axle with the ridged side up, then drive forward or backward slowly.
For kinetic rope: inspect for fraying before each use. Do not use a damaged kinetic rope — failure under load is violent.

Brief any trail partners on your recovery setup before you're in the mud figuring it out. Know where the recovery points are on your rig (the tow hooks at front and rear bumper on the JL are the primary attach points for soft shackles and hook connections).
Store recovery damper (sometimes called a recovery blanket) in an accessible location — it drapes over the strap between vehicles and reduces projectile risk if the strap parts under load.
pros: ARB RK11B covers the critical recovery scenarios in one purchase at a known quality level
Kinetic rope (Bubba Rope or ARB's included strap) is dramatically safer and more effective than static tow straps for unstuck recoveries
Maxtrax traction boards enable solo self-recovery — you don't need another vehicle on the trail to use them
Factor 55 FlatLink eliminates the steel hook projectile risk on a winch — mandatory upgrade for winch-equipped JLs
The full kit at $650 all-in is modest relative to the cost of a damaged rig or a tow truck
cons: Maxtrax MKII at $349/pair is the meaningful cost item in the kit; budget boards are available but less effective
ARB kit is comprehensive but includes some items you may not use (tree saver is only useful in wooded terrain) — piece-by-piece sourcing can optimize to your terrain type
Recovery skill matters more than hardware quality — invest time in learning proper recovery technique, not just collecting gear
Kinetic ropes must be kept clean and free of UV exposure during storage — degraded elasticity reduces effectiveness significantly
None of this gear replaces a winch for technical recovery situations; plan the kit as a foundation, not a substitute

title: Winch Selection for the JL Wrangler — 10,000 lb Minimum

parts.name: Warn M8000-S Winch (8,000 lb) — minimum for JLU

citations.title: Warn VR EVO 10-S Product Page
Warn Winch Selection Guide
Smittybilt X20 Gen2 Winch Overview

summary: A 10,000 lb winch is the correct floor for the JL — the JLU 4-door has a GVWR up to 5,300 lbs, and a winch rated at only 1.5x your vehicle weight is inadequate under real recovery conditions.
description:
The general rule is a winch rated at at least 1.5x the gross vehicle weight. The JL 2-door GVWR is approximately 4,500 lbs; the JLU 4-door sits at 4,900–5,300 lbs depending on trim and options. At those numbers, 8,000 lbs is technically marginal on a JLU and genuinely inadequate on a loaded Sahara with armor, a full tank, and gear. A 10,000 lb winch is the right answer for any JL build, and the cost difference between the Smittybilt X20 10K and an 8K unit is minimal.

The Warn VR EVO 10-S at $449 is the sweet spot for most JL builds. Warn's engineering reputation is earned — the EVO is Warn's entry-level sealed unit, which means the motor and control pack are protected from water and mud ingestion. Warn's customer support and parts availability are significantly better than budget brands, and the EVO's wireless remote is reliable. This is the first winch recommendation for anyone who hasn't winched before and wants a unit that behaves predictably.

The Smittybilt X20 Gen2 at $349 is the budget option. The X20 Gen2 is a notable improvement over the original X20 in build quality — sealed motor, IP67 rating, and wireless remote included. For a rig that uses the winch occasionally, the X20 Gen2 performs adequately. It won't hold up to heavy repeated use (multiple pulls per day in sustained mud) as well as the Warn, but for a JL that hits trails a few times a year, it's a functional choice.

The Warn Zeon 10-S at $1,099 is the premium choice for builds where the winch is a primary tool rather than a recovery backup. The Zeon uses a faster line speed, better motor cooling, and a free-spooling clutch mechanism that is noticeably smoother than the EVO. If you're running technical trails regularly and expect to use the winch as an active recovery tool — not just an emergency backup — the Zeon is worth the premium.

**Synthetic vs steel rope:** Every winch listed here ships with steel wire rope by default unless the model number ends in -S, which denotes synthetic. Synthetic rope (Dyneema or equivalent) is the correct choice for trail use — it doesn't store kinetic energy like steel, won't create a lethal snap-back if it parts under load, and is safe to touch with bare hands during rigging. The -S variants cost slightly more but the safety case for synthetic is not debatable. If your winch ships with steel, budget $80–$150 for a synthetic line upgrade.
steps: Confirm your front bumper has a winch-ready plate with mounting holes on the correct hole pattern for your winch model. Most JL aftermarket bumpers use a standard multi-pattern plate.
Thread the power leads from the winch drum along the mounting plate before bolting the winch down — much easier than fishing them after.
Mount the winch to the bumper plate. Torque mounting hardware to manufacturer spec — typically 40–50 ft-lb.
Route the positive and negative cables from the winch to the battery. Use the cable routing path that avoids the radiator and accessory belts.
Connect the positive lead directly to the battery positive post (with the inline fuse/fusible link that ships with the winch). Connect the negative lead to the battery negative post.
Install the fairlead (roller or Hawse — Hawse for synthetic rope, roller for steel) onto the bumper fairlead mount. Hawse fairleads require smooth Dyneema; roller fairleads are designed for steel.
Feed the rope through the fairlead, attach the hook or soft shackle to the drum end, and spool the rope onto the drum under light tension (have a helper pull the free end while you run the winch in).
Test in both directions before the trail. Confirm wireless remote function.
pros: Warn VR EVO 10-S delivers genuinely reliable performance at an accessible price point — the best value in this category
10,000 lb rating covers all JL and JLU GVWR variants with meaningful headroom
Synthetic rope (on -S models) eliminates the danger of steel snap-back under load
Wireless remote on all options listed is a meaningful safety upgrade — you can stay off the direct pull line while operating
Winch-ready bumpers make installation straightforward; no fabrication required
cons: Smittybilt X20 Gen2 is not the choice for rigs that winch regularly or in sustained heavy conditions — the motor will overheat faster than Warn units
Steel rope on non-S variants is a safety downgrade — budget for synthetic line upgrade if your winch ships with steel
Winch weight (35–70 lbs) adds to front-end nose weight; relevant on already-heavy builds with armor
The Warn M8000-S listed here is included for reference but is below the recommended minimum for a fully-loaded JLU — use 10K as the floor
Electrical connections must be properly fused and routed — a poorly done winch install is a fire risk; take the time to do the wiring correctly

title: Alignment After Lift — JL-Specific Specs

parts.name: Synergy adjustable front lower control arms (pair)

citations.title: JL Wrangler Alignment Specs Discussion
Basic DIY JL Front End Alignment — WAYALIFE

summary: A 2"+ lift on a JL drops caster below the 4° safety floor; you need adjustable lower control arms to bring it back to 4.5°–5.5° or the front end will wander at highway speed.
description:
The JL runs more positive caster from the factory than the JK did — Sport models target 5.35°, Sahara 5.05°, Rubicon 4.80°, with toe at 0.20° ± 0.15° total and camber at -0.25°. That extra caster is what makes the JL feel less twitchy than the JK at highway speed. The problem: lift kits rotate the axle pinion up, and on a solid-axle Jeep that means caster goes down by roughly 1° per inch of lift. Two inches of lift and you're at 3°–4° caster, below the Jeep service manual's 4.0° minimum. That's when the wandering and floaty steering complaints start.

What can and can't be adjusted: toe is the only spec you can change with stock parts — loosen the tie rod adjuster sleeve clamps, rotate the sleeve, retighten. Camber on a solid axle is fixed by the axle housing; there is no adjustment. Caster requires changing the angle of the axle, which means adjustable lower control arms (cheapest path) or adjustable upper and lower arms (best path for big lifts). The lowers reposition the axle fore-aft; the uppers rotate the pinion. With just lowers you can claw back about 2°–3° of caster. With both, you can fully restore stock geometry.

Target settings for a lifted JL: caster 4.5°–5.5°, total toe 0.15°–0.20° toe-in, camber whatever the axle gives (don't worry about it). Higher caster up to 6° feels tighter but eats tires faster and adds steering effort. Below 4° you risk wander and death-wobble vulnerability.

The tape-measure toe check works at home: roll the Jeep forward 6 feet to settle the suspension, measure between the front of the tires at hub height, then between the rear of the tires at the same height. The front number should be 1/16" to 1/8" smaller than the rear. Adjust the tie rod sleeve to dial it in. A proper alignment shop will charge $100–$140 to do this with a rack and verify caster, which is worth doing after any lift.
steps: Confirm the lift is fully installed, all control arm bolts torqued at ride height.
Drive the Jeep 20–50 miles to settle bushings.
Bring to alignment shop with a printout of target specs (caster 4.5°–5.5°, total toe 0.15°–0.20° toe-in).
If caster is below 4°, do not road-test at highway speed — install adjustable lower control arms first.
With adjustable lowers, lengthen them to push axle rearward, increasing caster.
With adjustable uppers, shorten them to rotate pinion up.
Have shop re-measure after each adjustment.
Set total toe to 0.15"–0.20" toe-in.
Center the steering wheel by adjusting equal turns on each tie rod end.
Test drive — straight steering, no pull, no wander at 65 mph.
pros: Restores correct caster after a lift
Eliminates highway wander
Reduces death wobble risk by keeping caster above 4°
Adjustable arms also re-center axle fore-aft
cons: Caster correction requires aftermarket arms
Camber is non-adjustable — you live with what the axle gives you
Big lifts (4"+) need both upper and lower adjustable arms
Setting caster too high eats tires and adds steering effort

title: Death Wobble on JL — Different from JK but Same Root Causes

parts.name: Synergy JL HD adjustable track bar

citations.title: NHTSA Recall 18V-675 — JL track bar bracket weld
JLWranglerForums — Track Bar Bracket Weld Recall
4xeForums — Lower ball joint TSB 02-004-21 build dates 9/16/20–8/4/21

summary: Death wobble on a JL has the same root cause as the JK — loose or worn front-end components triggered by a bump — but the JL adds three platform-specific suspects: the recalled 2018 track bar bracket weld (NHTSA 18V-675), the aluminum steering gear box (TSB 08-074-20), and the lower ball joint TSB on trucks built between September 2020 and August 2021. Check those three first, then inspect the rest of the front end like a JK.
description:
The JL inherited the JK's solid front axle with a linked drag-link-and-tie-rod setup. Same geometry, same failure mode. What changed is what Jeep tried to do to fix the JK's reputation — and some of those changes created new failure points.

**The 2018 track bar bracket recall.** Early JLs (built before December 2018) had a frame-side track bar bracket where the weld was placed off the seam. Under load the bracket separated from the frame, and the axle could shift freely. NHTSA recall 18V-675 covers the fix. If your JL is a 2018 build, run the VIN through NHTSA's recall lookup before doing anything else — if the recall has not been performed, the dealer fixes it free.

**The aluminum steering gear box.** 2018 JLs left the factory with an aluminum steering gear box that flexed under high steering input. TSB 08-074-20 replaces it with a steel unit. Symptom is vague on-center steering and wobble that returns after every alignment. Dealer handles this under warranty for affected VINs.

**Lower ball joints, builds 9/16/20 to 8/4/21.** TSB 02-004-21-REV A covers lower front ball joints that loosen prematurely and trigger death wobble. If your JL was built in that window, the dealer inspects and replaces them free of charge.

**Then it's a JK inspection.** With recalls and TSBs cleared, run the same systematic front-end inspection you would on a JK. Get the wheels off the ground, rock each tire 12/6 and 9/3 for ball joint and tie rod end play, watch every joint while a helper turns the steering wheel, and check track bar bolt torque (110 ft-lb axle / 125 ft-lb frame on JL). Re-torque after any wheeling trip. A stabilizer cannot cure death wobble on a JL any more than it can on a JK — fix the root cause.

**A note on aftermarket fixes.** Some owners install a dual-pin track bar bracket (Synergy, Metalcloak) when the frame-side bracket has wallowed even after a recall fix. Adjustable track bars from Synergy and RockJock allow re-centering the axle after a lift, which matters because off-center geometry amplifies wobble. Heavy-duty tie rod kits (RockJock Currectlync JL CE-9701JL, Steer Smarts Yeti XD) replace the factory bent rod with a straight DOM tube that resists impact-bend on rocks.
steps: Run your VIN through NHTSA's recall lookup at nhtsa.gov/recalls. Address recall 18V-675 (track bar bracket) if it shows open.
Ask the dealer to check TSB 08-074-20 (steering gear box) and TSB 02-004-21 (ball joints) against your build date. Both are dealer-paid if eligible.
With recalls cleared, put the front wheels on jack stands. Rock each tire at 12/6 and 9/3 — diagnose worn ball joints vs. tie rod ends.
Have a helper turn the wheel slowly while you watch each joint. Independent slop is a worn part.
Verify track bar bolt torque: 110 ft-lb at the axle, 125 ft-lb at the frame.
Inspect track bar bushings and bracket. Pry-test the bar at the axle bracket for any movement.
Replace worn components, re-torque, alignment shop afterward.
Road test gradually toward the speed wobble occurred at, with bump tests in between.
pros: Recalls and TSBs are free at the dealer
Solves the wobble at the source rather than masking it
Catches related wear before it becomes a roadside breakdown
cons: Diagnosis still takes a couple of hours
Aluminum gear box replacement is dealer-only on out-of-warranty trucks ($900+)
Lifted JLs with 35"+ tires need geometry correction in addition to part replacement
Some owners report repeat wobble even after full front-end replacement on early 2018 trucks — track bar bracket reinforcement may be required

title: Tie Rod and Drag Link Replacement

parts.name: Apex Chassis 2.5 Ton ProLock Tie Rod & Drag Link Kit (Steel)
Synergy Heavy Duty Chromoly Tie Rod (JL)
Steer Smarts YETI XD JL Drag Link

citations.title: Apex Chassis KIT115 JL Steering Kit
JL Wrangler Tie Rod & Drag Link Guide

summary: The JL's factory steering was the subject of a 2019 service campaign and is still the weakest link on lifted trucks — a heavy-duty tie rod and matching drag link tighten the front end and stop the wandering most owners complain about.
description:
Jeep updated the JL tie rod under service bulletin W30 because the original two-piece design developed play that drove an epidemic of loose, vague steering. Even the updated factory tie rod is fine for stock trucks on stock tires, but it's the first thing to fail once you add 35"+ tires, a lift, or any meaningful trail use. The drag link uses the same forged-end design and tends to develop the same play a few thousand miles later.

Three configurations cover most builds. A complete steel kit like Apex Chassis KIT115 ($900) gets you a 2.5-ton tie rod and drag link with greasable forged ends in one box — that's the simplest upgrade if you want everything done in a single afternoon. Synergy and Steer Smarts both sell standalone chromoly tie rods around $500–$550, which is the right call if your drag link is still tight and only the tie rod has play. For the loaded overland or rockcrawler build, Steer Smarts YETI XD covers both pieces with 30 mm ball joints at the top of the price range.

Aluminum tie rods are sold for the JL but corrosion at the sleeve threads and stripped jam nuts have shown up enough times in the forums that most experienced JL builders steer clear unless weight is the absolute priority.

Torque specs matter on this truck. The knuckle nuts are 47 ft-lb, the pitman arm nut is 77 ft-lb, and the steering stabilizer bolt/nut are 50/55 ft-lb. Jam nuts on 3/4-16 sleeves start at 180 ft-lb — don't guess them.
steps: Park level, chock rear wheels, loosen front lug nuts, jack the front axle and put it on stands.
Remove both front wheels for clearance.
Measure the tie rod and drag link center-to-center lengths and write them down.
Remove the steering stabilizer to give yourself room to swing.

Pop the cotter pins, remove the knuckle nuts (tie rod) and pitman arm nut (drag link), and separate with a proper tie rod separator. Avoid pickle forks here — they wreck the boots if you plan to keep any factory pieces as backups.
Pre-assemble the new tie rod and drag link to match the recorded lengths.
Install the tie rod first. Torque knuckle nuts to 47 ft-lb, then continue tightening to align cotter pin slots. Install new cotter pins.
Install the drag link. Torque the pitman arm nut to 77 ft-lb and the knuckle end to 47 ft-lb.
Tighten all sleeve clamps or jam nuts to the manufacturer's spec (180 ft-lb minimum for 3/4-16). Grease zerks.
Reinstall the steering stabilizer (50 ft-lb bolt, 55 ft-lb nut), wheels (95 ft-lb lugs), and get an alignment.
pros: Cures the post-W30 wandering on lifted trucks
Greasable rebuildable ends
Works with the factory steering damper
cons: Best kits run nearly $1,000
Alignment required
Aluminum bargain options can corrode and strip

title: Budget Lift Kit — Spacers and Entry Springs (≤$600)

parts.name: Rough Country 2" Lift Kit N3 Shocks (JL)

citations.title: Teraflex JL Suspension Spacer Kit Product Page
Rough Country Jeep JL Lift Kits

summary: A budget lift on the JL clears 33s with room to spare and lifts the stance without touching the geometry — but you are making trade-offs, and you should know what they are before you buy.
description:
Coil spacers and entry-level spring kits work on the JL because the factory suspension geometry is already reasonably dialed for street and mild trail use. Up to 1.5–2 inches, you can add height without significant caster correction or control arm adjustment — the JL's geometry tolerates that range better than the JK did. The Teraflex 1.5" spacer kit is the cleanest execution of this approach: it uses a proper spacer that mounts between the coil and the perch rather than a puck shoved in the spring, which limits bind. Daystar's 2" coil spacers are the same idea at a lower price point but ship as raw spacers with no additional hardware — fine for overland rigs that don't see aggressive flexing.

The Rough Country 2" kit steps up to replacement springs and includes N3 shocks, which is a meaningfully better outcome for the money than spacers alone. The shocks are not premium, but they are better valved for the lifted ride height than the factory shocks pushed beyond their intended range. If you're shopping this tier because budget is a hard constraint, the Rough Country kit is the most complete option under $250. Just know that the control arm angles are not corrected at 2" — you will notice mild vibration at highway speed in some rigs, and death wobble risk increases if your front-end components (tie rod, track bar, ball joints) are anything less than perfect.

What is not included at this price point: adjustable control arms, caster correction, geometry-matched sway bar end links, or track bar correction. Those items matter more as lift height increases and as trail use intensifies. A 1.5"–2" spacer lift on a mild-trail or overlanding JL is a defensible choice. A 2" spacer lift on a rig that sees rocky terrain regularly is asking for accelerated wear on your front-end components.
steps: Chock rear wheels, loosen front lug nuts, then lift the front of the vehicle and support on jack stands under the frame rails.
Remove front wheels and set aside.
Support the front axle with the floor jack — don't let it hang on the CV axles.
Remove the front sway bar end links (or disconnect them if using detachable links).
Slowly lower the axle to relieve spring tension. Pull the factory coil springs.
Install spacers per manufacturer instructions. For Daystar puck-style spacers, seat them fully on the upper spring perch before seating the spring beneath.
Reinstall springs, raise the axle to seat the spring, reconnect sway bar end links.
Reinstall wheels, torque lug nuts to 100 ft-lb.
Repeat for rear axle: support frame, lower axle, swap rear coils or install rear spacers.
Lower vehicle fully to ground, then torque all suspension fasteners to spec with the vehicle at ride height (critical — torquing at full droop will bind the bushings).
Drive to an alignment shop within 50 miles. A 2" lift on the JL will require at minimum a front toe alignment check.
pros: Lowest cost entry into a lifted JL — Daystar spacers at $129 are hard to beat for a mild stance lift
Bolt-on installation with basic tools; no specialty equipment beyond a spring compressor
Retains factory ride quality at the 1.5" range
Rough Country kit includes shocks that are better matched to the new ride height than factory units
Reversible — you can return to stock by removing spacers
cons: No caster correction or geometry adjustment — factory control arm angles are not changed
Increased highway vibration risk, especially on JLs with any front-end wear
Spacer lifts stress the CV axles at full droop — more aggressive trail use will accelerate axle wear
Rough Country shocks are adequate but not trail-capable; they will not hold up to repeated hard hits on rocky trails
Does not clear 35" tires without fender trimming on non-Rubicon trims
Not suitable as a foundation for future lift height increases — spacers compound angle problems already present

title: JL Coil Spring Replacement

citations.title: TORQUE SPECS — JL Wrangler Reference Guide
Jeep JL Wrangler Torque Specs — Metalcloak
Complete Torque Values for Jeep JL Wrangler

summary: JL coil swaps are bolt-in if you drop the axle far enough to clear the coils — the catch is torquing control arm and track bar bolts at ride height, not full droop, or you'll preload the bushings and chew through them.
description:
The JL inherited the JK's coil-sprung solid-axle layout but tightened the geometry — control arms are stiffer, bushings are different, and the front track bar mounts higher on the frame. The coil swap procedure itself is among the most approachable suspension jobs on the JL because nothing is captured: drop the axle, pull the spring out the top, swap, reassemble. No spring compressor needed for OEM-height or 2.5" coils.

The mistake people make on JLs is final-torquing the control arm and track bar bolts with the axle drooping on jack stands. Polyurethane and rubber bushings establish their neutral position based on where the suspension was sitting when the bolt got torqued. Tighten them at full droop, and they're pre-loaded against the resting suspension position the entire time the Jeep is on the ground. The result is harsh ride, premature bushing wear, and rubber bushings that crack within 20K miles. The fix is to either set the axle at ride height on a drive-on lift or to set everything to snug, lower the Jeep, then crawl underneath with a torque wrench.

Coil selection on the JL splits into three lanes. Stock-height replacement (Mopar OEM, $80–$120 per spring) is for owners whose original coils sagged or who lost one to corrosion. 2.5" leveling coils (Rough Country, Teraflex, Mopar 2" lift kit) get you to 35" tires with no other geometry tricks. 3.5" coils (Metalcloak Game-Changer, Rock Krawler) start to need extended brake lines, adjustable track bar, and adjustable control arms to keep the front end pointed straight. Don't run 3.5" coils with stock arms and the stock track bar — bump steer and pulling-to-one-side will follow.

JL coils are progressive-wound on most aftermarket sets. The bottom coils are heavier so they support the rig's curb weight; the top coils are lighter so they compress earlier under small bumps. This is why a Rubicon front spring will sit different heights on a Sport versus a 4xe — same spring, different weight on it. Weigh your front axle if you're swapping models. The 4xe carries about 200 lb more on the front axle than a gas Sport.

The bumpstop retainer cup bolt at the top of the coil pocket is hand-tight only; don't crank it. The spring retainer clip at the lower coil seat takes 16 ft-lb. Top shock bolts are 17 ft-lb with a small 1/4" wrench on the shaft to keep it from spinning. Front lower shock bolt is 70 ft-lb (M14). Track bar at axle: 125 ft-lb. Track bar at frame: 55 ft-lb. Control arm bolts at axle and frame: 125 ft-lb, torqued at ride height.
steps: Crack lug nuts (21mm) on the corner you're working. Lift the front of the Jeep, support on stands under the frame rails.
Remove front wheels. Support the axle under the differential with a floor jack.
Disconnect both front sway bar end links at the axle (15mm). On Rubicons with electronic disconnect, cycle the disconnect first, then unbolt.
Disconnect the lower shock bolts (18mm) at the axle.
Disconnect the track bar at the axle bracket (21mm, 125 ft-lb to reinstall).
Slowly lower the floor jack to drop the axle. The coils will lose tension as the axle drops 5–6 inches.
Remove the spring retainer clip (13mm bolt, 16 ft-lb to reinstall).
Pull the coil out the top with the bumpstop still in the bumpstop cup.
Install the new coil — make sure it seats in the upper pocket isolator and the lower spring perch.
Reinstall the retainer clip (16 ft-lb).
Jack the axle back up. Reconnect shock, track bar, and sway bar links — all to "snug" only.
Lower the Jeep to the ground, drive 20 feet to settle bushings.
Final-torque control arms (125 ft-lb), track bar (125 ft-lb at axle, 55 at frame), sway bar links (70 ft-lb) at ride height.
Get an alignment. Caster spec: 4.5°–6.0°.
pros: No spring compressor needed for stock-height or 2.5" coils
Bolt-in swap with common metric tools
Wide aftermarket options from $200 to $600
2.5" coils clear 35s on a Rubicon with no other parts
cons: Torquing at full droop wrecks bushings — easy mistake to make
4xe weights front axle differently than gas; coil choice matters
3.5"+ lifts need adjustable track bar, adjustable control arms, longer brake lines
Always plan an alignment after the swap

title: Expedition and Rock Lift — Long-Arm Full System ($2,000+)

parts.name: Rock Krawler 3.5" Mid-Arm Stage 2 Lift System (JL)

citations.title: Rock Krawler JL Wrangler Suspension Systems
EVO Manufacturing JL Enforcer Lift System
Synergy Manufacturing JL Long-Arm Suspension

summary: A long-arm or full expedition system on the JL is a major build commitment — you're changing the fundamental geometry of the rig, and the labor bill alone can approach the kit cost if you don't do it yourself.
description:
Long-arm suspension replaces the factory short control arms with longer arms that attach further outboard on the axle. The result is dramatically better flex, more stable geometry at full droop, and the ability to run 37"–40" tires without fighting the suspension for clearance. The JL responds exceptionally well to this treatment because the factory trackbar and control arm mount positions were already better designed than the JK's — you're not correcting as many fundamentally compromised factory choices, you're extending a good foundation.

The Rock Krawler 3.5" Mid-Arm Stage 2 is the benchmark in this category. Rock Krawler's JL system uses a mid-arm geometry — longer than the factory short arms but shorter than a full long-arm — that delivers 80% of the flex benefit without requiring the crossmember relocation that true long-arm kits demand. The result is a system that a capable home builder can install without frame modification. At $3,876, you get replacement coils, Fox 2.0 Performance shocks, adjustable control arms, and all geometry correction hardware.

The EVO Mfg Enforcer is the value entry into full-system territory. EVO's approach is aggressive fitment spec and domestic manufacturing, and the Enforcer is genuinely a rock-build kit — the sway bar end links and front coils are spec'd for heavy hits and axle articulation, not highway comfort. If your JL is primarily a trail rig and you don't care about plush road manners, the Enforcer at $2,899 is money well spent. The Synergy 4" system is the premium build choice — Synergy's fitment tolerances and hardware quality are exceptional, and the 4" height opens up 40" tire territory on a Rubicon with portal axles.

**4xe owners:** The rear battery pack on the Wrangler 4xe changes the rear suspension geometry and limits available rear lift. Most full systems are not 4xe compatible without modification — EVO Mfg explicitly lists 4xe compatibility; Rock Krawler and Synergy require direct confirmation with tech support before purchasing. Do not assume a standard JL kit works on a 4xe.

**Warranty:** Any lift over 2" installed without factory authorization voids the factory powertrain warranty. This is not a scare tactic — it's documented in Jeep's warranty policy. On a rig this heavily modified, most owners budget for extended aftermarket coverage or accept the trade-off.
steps: Read the full installation manual before buying any additional parts — full systems often require supplemental hardware (specific bump stops, brake line extensions, front diff drop if running a non-Rubicon Dana 30) that ships separately.
Plan for a full weekend minimum. 16–24 hours is realistic for a first-time installation without professional help.
Lift and support the vehicle safely. Long-arm installs often require full body clearance — use tall jack stands or a lift.
Remove wheels, disconnect shocks, and disconnect all factory control arms front and rear.
Remove factory coil springs. If the kit requires crossmember modification or skid plate removal, complete that work before reinstalling anything.
Install new front lower and upper control arms per kit sequence. Torque in the correct order — wrong sequence will preload bushings incorrectly.
Install replacement coil springs front and rear.
Install new shocks. If the kit includes external reservoir shocks, route the reservoir lines before buttoning up.
Install geometry correction hardware: trackbar brackets, caster correction plates, sway bar brackets.
Install new sway bar end links (adjustable or quick-disconnect per kit).
Route any extended brake lines if included — do not reuse factory lines if kit specifies new ones.
Reinstall skid plates and crossmembers.
Reinstall wheels, lower vehicle to ground.
Torque all fasteners to spec at ride height — this step is non-negotiable on a full system.
Drive to a reputable alignment shop with lift experience. Request caster adjustment be set to kit spec, not factory spec.
pros: Maximum flex and articulation — rock crawling capability approaches dedicated trail rig levels
Clears 37"–40" tires depending on kit and axle configuration
Premium shocks included (Fox 2.0 or equivalent) are genuinely trail-capable, not entry-level
Rock Krawler mid-arm approach delivers most flex benefits without requiring frame modification
Well-engineered geometry correction from these brands means predictable, stable handling on-road
These kits are designed as final build platforms, not starting points — you don't need to upgrade further
cons: Cost is significant — $2,900–$4,300 for hardware alone, add $1,000–$2,000 labor if shop-installed
Install complexity is high; this is a two-day project for an experienced home builder, longer for first-timers
Voids factory warranty on any JL not past the warranty period
4xe compatibility is not universal — verify directly with the manufacturer before purchasing
Long-arm kits require a dedicated alignment shop visit and alignment to kit specs, not factory specs
At 3.5"–4" lift, steering geometry changes are significant enough that an SAS (steering angle sensor) calibration may be required depending on trim level
Heavier and stiffer springs reduce ride compliance compared to factory — the JL will feel truck-like on pavement

title: JL Lift Kit Options — What Changed from JK

parts.name: Mopar 2" Lift Kit with Fox shocks

citations.title: Aftermarket JL Lift Kit suspension options master list
The Ultimate Jeep Wrangler Lift Kit Comparison
Mopar 2" Lift Kit Fox Series for JLU

summary: The JL keeps the JK's coil-sprung five-link layout but uses different spring rates, a wider front track bar angle, and a more expensive geometry-correction price tag — budget about $200 extra over a JK build for the same lift height.
description:
The JL chassis carries forward the five-link front and rear coil suspension from the JK. So you can still pick from spacer lifts, spring lifts, mid-arm kits, and long-arm kits. What changed is the geometry-correction tax. Caster on the JL drops faster per inch of lift, and the OEM geometry-correction bracket from Mopar/aftermarket costs around $200 for a JL versus about $90 for the JK. Plan for that.

Spacer lifts (1.25"–2") are bolt-on coil spacers. Cheap, fast, and they keep the OEM ride. Mopar's own 2" kit with Fox shocks at $1,599 is a popular middle path because it's covered if you also lease the Jeep. AEV's 2.5" Dualsport RT ($1,379) is the expedition-grade spring lift for owners running heavy bumpers and a roof rack. Rock Krawler's 3.5" Mid-Arm Stage 2 ($3,876) goes furthest with adjustable lower arms, adjustable track bars, and corrected sway bar links — that's a 37" tire build.

The 4xe complicates lift selection: the rear battery pack changes ride height, and lifts under 2" usually keep the factory shocks; lifts at 2.5"+ require longer shocks specced for 4xe rear hardware. Confirm any kit you buy lists 4xe compatibility on the box.

Sway bar links changed in 2024 — Jeep updated hardware specs, so a link from a 2018 kit may not fit a 2024 build correctly. Check year-specific fitment before ordering.

Tire fitment guide: 33" tires fit a stock JL with no lift if you trim the front fender liner. 35s need 2"–2.5" of lift plus 17"+ wheels with proper backspacing. 37s need 3.5"+ of lift on a non-Rubicon, or a Dynatrac/AEV kit on a Rubicon designed for that height.
steps: Decide tire size first — that drives lift height, not the other way around.
Pick a kit type: spacer (cheap), spring lift (OEM-style ride), or mid-arm/long-arm (best geometry).
Verify 4xe and model-year compatibility with the kit vendor.
Order geometry correction (brackets or adjustable arms) for any lift over 1.5".
Pull stock springs, install new components per kit instructions.
Re-center axle with the front track bar, then set toe to 1/16"–1/8" toe-in.
Get a rack alignment — JL alignment specs are tighter than JK.
pros: Wide range of OEM-blessed and aftermarket options
4xe-specific kits available
Backed by stronger factory steering than late JK
cons: Geometry correction costs more than equivalent JK parts
4xe lifts can void some factory warranty coverage
Sway bar link hardware varies by year — verify before buying

title: Mid-Tier Lift Kit — Spring Lift with Geometry Correction ($600–$2,000)

parts.name: Mopar 2" Lift Kit with Fox Shocks (JL)

citations.title: JKS Manufacturing JL Wrangler Lift Systems
Mopar Jeep Performance Parts — JL Lift Kit
Teraflex JL Performance Spacer Lift System

summary: The mid-tier lift is where the JL gets genuinely capable — real geometry correction, 35s without drama, and a ride that holds up on trail — but the JL costs more to do right than the JK did, and that gap matters when you're budgeting.
description:
The JL's suspension geometry is more complex than the JK's. The trackbar mount positions, control arm angles, and coil spring rates were all updated, and aftermarket lift manufacturers had to start from scratch rather than adapt JK geometry. That's why a properly executed 2.5" lift on a JL typically runs $200–$400 more than the equivalent JK kit from the same brand. It's not padding — the geometry correction hardware is different and the spring rates are re-engineered for the JL's heavier body-on-frame structure.

The Mopar 2" Fox lift kit is the standout option if warranty coverage matters to you. It's the only JL lift kit that preserves the factory bumper-to-bumper warranty when dealer-installed, and the Fox shocks included are legitimate trail shocks — not baseline fill valves. The tradeoff is price: at $1,599 installed, you're paying for peace of mind. It also tops out at 2" with this kit, which gets you to 35s on Rubicon or near there on non-Rubicon with trimming.

The JKS 2.5" system is the value choice for a trail-focused build. JKS includes their quicker-disconnect sway bar links, which are a genuine upgrade over stock — you can disconnect in under 30 seconds trailside without tools. At 2.5", this kit clears 35s comfortably across all JL trims with minor fender liner trimming. The Teraflex 2.5" system is the budget-ceiling option in this tier: it's a spacer-based approach rather than a full spring replacement, so you get the height and some geometry correction, but the ride quality doesn't improve as much as it does with the JKS or Mopar kits.

Note on the 2024 JL: updated sway bar link hardware was introduced. Verify kit compatibility with your specific year before purchasing — some pre-2024 kits require updated hardware for 2024 fitment.
steps: Stage all hardware and read the full instruction sheet before picking up a wrench — JL lift kits have a non-obvious sequence for control arm adjustments that varies by brand.
Loosen all lug nuts with the vehicle on the ground.
Lift the vehicle at the frame rails and support securely on jack stands. Lift front and rear separately, do not attempt to lift all four corners at once.
Support the front axle with a floor jack.
Remove front wheels.
Disconnect sway bar end links.
Remove front shocks — mark factory ride height before removal if adjustable replacement shocks are included.
Compress or relieve tension on front coil springs and remove. Install replacement springs per kit instructions.
Install new front shocks.
Install trackbar drop bracket if included (critical for maintaining steering geometry at 2"+ lift on the JL).
Install adjustable control arms if included, or verify factory control arm length is within kit spec — do not assume factory length is acceptable without checking the kit instructions.
Reinstall sway bar end links (new links from kit, or JKS quick-disconnects if included).
Reinstall wheels. Lower front to ground.
Repeat process for rear: support axle, remove rear shocks, swap rear springs, install rear shocks. Install any rear control arm adjusters or trackbar corrections per kit.
Lower vehicle fully to ground.
Torque all suspension fasteners to spec with the vehicle at ride height — not at full droop.
Drive straight to an alignment shop. A full four-wheel alignment is required, not optional.
pros: Clears 35s on all JL trims with minor trimming; 37s possible on Rubicon with additional front-end clearance work
Geometry correction hardware included means much lower vibration and steering wander risk vs spacer lifts
Mopar kit preserves factory warranty when dealer-installed — only lift option that does
JKS quick-disconnect sway bar links are a trail-day quality-of-life upgrade included in the kit
Full spring replacement (JKS/Mopar) improves overall ride quality compared to factory springs at lifted height
Solid foundation for future upgrades — lockers, armor, heavier tires
cons: Substantially more expensive than JK equivalent kits due to JL-specific geometry engineering
Trackbar drop bracket required at 2"+ adds hardware and potential long-term rust/fatigue point
Professional alignment is mandatory and adds $80–$120 to the total cost
Teraflex spacer system in this tier doesn't improve ride quality as much as spring-replacement alternatives
4xe owners: rear lift height interacts with the rear battery pack — verify 4xe compatibility before purchasing; not all mid-tier kits explicitly support 4xe
Full install is a long day — plan for 8–10 hours if this is your first JL lift

title: Shock Absorber Replacement

parts.name: Bilstein B8 5100 Front Shock (0-2" lift, JL Unlimited)
Bilstein B8 5100 Rear Shock (2-3" lift, JL Unlimited)
Bilstein B8 5100 Rear Shock (3-4.5" lift, JL)
Fox 2.0 Performance Series IFP Rear Shock (JL)

citations.title: Bilstein 5100 Front JL Unlimited 33-292625
Bilstein 5100 Rear JL 2-3" lift 33-292632
Fox 2.0 Performance Rear IFP Shock JL

summary: Replace JL shocks when they leak, fade on long trails, or no longer settle after a bump — match shock length to your current lift height, not your future plans.
description:
Stock JL shocks are tuned soft for on-road comfort. They fade quickly on washboard, body-control gets sloppy after 60,000 miles, and the rear shocks are usually the first to leak. If you've added a lift, the stock shocks are likely topped out before full droop — meaning you've got internal damage even if they aren't visibly leaking.

The decision tree is short. Stock height and want a better ride? Bilstein 5100 monotubes (33-292625 front, 33-316321 rear for 0-1.5" lift, 33-292632 rear for 2-3" lift) are bolt-in upgrades at around $110 per corner. Lifted 2-3"? Same Bilstein 5100s in the lifted length. Lifted 3"+? Step up to remote-reservoir shocks like Fox 2.0 Performance Series IFP, Bilstein 8112, or King 2.5 — your shocks will see more heat and travel.

Avoid the temptation to put a 4" lift shock on a stock vehicle. The shock will top out at full extension, which damages the internal valving and gives you a harsh ride at any extension.

Install is the simplest suspension job on the JL. Unlike spring or control arm work, shock replacement doesn't touch alignment geometry. One side at a time, no spring tension released. Stock JL shock mounting uses 18mm and 21mm fasteners. Mopar service spec for shock-to-axle bolt is 75 ft-lb, shock-to-frame upper bolt is 60 ft-lb — confirm against the included instructions for your specific shock as some aftermarket units use different hardware.

Pre-extend new shocks before installing them upright (most monotubes ship gas-charged at full extension, but pre-cycling them by hand helps seat the valving). Don't install a shock upside down — the IFP gas charge needs to be at the top for proper damping.
steps: Park on level ground; chock the opposite wheel.
Lift one corner; place jack stand under the frame, leaving the axle hanging.
Remove the wheel.
Spray penetrating oil on both shock mounting bolts; let sit 5 minutes.
Unbolt the lower shock bolt (at the axle bracket).
Unbolt the upper shock bolt (at the frame mount).
Compress the old shock by hand and remove.
Cycle the new shock 3–5 times by hand to seat valving.
Install upper bolt first (loose), then lower bolt.
Torque to spec — typically 75 ft-lb lower, 60 ft-lb upper (verify with your shock's instructions).
Reinstall wheel; torque lug nuts to 130 ft-lb.
Repeat for remaining corners.
Drive 50 miles, then re-check shock bolt torque (rubber bushings settle).
pros: Cheapest meaningful ride upgrade
No alignment needed after
Bolt-in, no spring compressor required
Bilstein 5100s last 60,000+ miles on daily-driver JLs
cons: Wrong-length shocks for your lift cause internal damage
Stock shock mount bolts can seize after Phoenix heat cycles — penetrant first
Remote-reservoir shocks need clearance routing for the reservoir hose
Rear shocks on Unlimited 4-doors are tight to the gas tank — work from below

summary: Shock absorber quality is the single most important determinant of ride quality on a lifted JL — the springs set the height, but the shocks control everything else, and factory shocks are not built to the standard these vehicles deserve on trail.
description:
The JL Wrangler's factory shocks are adequate for the street-use case the platform was originally calibrated for. The moment you lift the rig, run heavier tires, or take it onto washboard roads and rocky terrain, the factory shocks are out of their designed range. They overheat on sustained trail use, blow through their travel on repeated hits, and provide a choppy ride that fatigues the driver and stresses the rest of the suspension. Aftermarket shocks are not a luxury upgrade — on a trail-going JL, they're a functional requirement.

**Shock length matters at lift height.** Factory shocks are compressed at lifted ride height because they weren't designed for it. Running factory shocks at 2" of lift means they spend most of their travel compressed — you lose bump travel, which is the travel direction that absorbs hits. Aftermarket shocks for lifted JLs are spec'd for the lifted ride height and provide correct travel distribution. When ordering, specify your lift height. Most brands offer shocks in multiple length ranges to match 0"–1.5", 1.5"–3", and 3"+ lift applications.

The Bilstein 5100 at $675 for a set of four is the benchmark value option. Bilstein's monotube design provides more consistent damping than twin-tube designs (the factory shocks are twin-tube) and the 5100 is a proven choice with extensive real-world use on JL platforms. The 5100 is not adjustable, which is a limitation for builds that want to tune the ride between street and trail configurations.

The Fox 2.0 Performance at $850 moves up to Fox's internal floating piston (IFP) monotube design. The IFP separates the oil from the nitrogen charge, which maintains consistent damping across temperature ranges better than non-IFP designs. On sustained trail use — long washboard sections, repeated rocky hits — the Fox 2.0 holds its tune longer than the Bilstein 5100. The Performance Elite at $1,050 adds remote reservoir capability (on some variants) or an externally adjustable compression knob, which lets you dial the front shocks for street or trail on the fly.

King OEM Performance at $1,325 for a set of four is the premium choice for builds that prioritize shock performance above all else. King's quality is exceptional and their valving is notably better than Fox or Bilstein at managing high-frequency small hits (the kind that cause driver fatigue on long trail runs) while still handling big impacts. If your JL is primarily a trail rig and you spend significant time in the vehicle on technical terrain, King shocks deliver a noticeably different experience.

**4xe rear shocks:** The Wrangler 4xe's rear battery pack changes the rear spring and shock mounting geometry. The rear shocks on the 4xe are different lengths than the standard JL rear units. When ordering shocks for a 4xe, specify 4xe rear fitment explicitly — most brands offer 4xe-specific rear shocks, but the front shocks are the same as the standard JL.
steps: Lift and support the vehicle on jack stands at the frame rails. Support the axle with a floor jack.
For each shock: remove the upper mount bolt/nut first, then the lower.
Note the factory shock mounting orientation before removal — some JL shocks are not fully symmetrical and must be installed in a specific direction.
Compare old shock length to new shock extended and collapsed length. Confirm the new shock is the correct length for your lift height.
Install new shocks. Start upper mount first, then lower.
Torque upper mount to manufacturer spec (typically 55–65 ft-lb). Torque lower mount to spec (typically 70–80 ft-lb on the lower axle pin).
For adjustable shocks (Fox Performance Elite, some King variants): set the adjuster to the starting position recommended by the manufacturer before the first trail run.
After installation, cycle the suspension through full travel to confirm no binding and correct range of motion.
Re-torque all shock hardware after the first 500 miles.
pros: Bilstein 5100 delivers a significant ride improvement over factory shocks at an accessible price point
Fox 2.0 Performance maintains consistent damping on sustained trail use better than the Bilstein 5100
King OEM Performance shocks are the clear winner for managing high-frequency trail feedback and driver fatigue
Correct-length aftermarket shocks restore proper travel distribution at lifted ride height — factory shocks can't do this
Shock upgrade is one of the most accessible technical installs on the JL — straightforward bolt-on with basic tools
cons: Bilstein 5100 is not adjustable — no ability to tune between street and trail configurations
Fox Performance Elite adjustability is meaningful but requires understanding of what the adjustment does; incorrect settings can degrade performance
King shocks at $1,325 are a significant investment — prioritize against other build items unless shocks are the bottleneck
4xe rear fitment is different from standard JL — must specify 4xe compatibility when ordering rear shocks
All aftermarket shocks require correct length spec matched to your lift height — ordering the wrong length results in incorrect travel distribution

title: Running 37" Tires on the JL — Rubicon vs Non-Rubicon Fitment

citations.title: Jeep JL Wrangler Tire Fitment Guide — Quadratec
BFGoodrich KM3 Tire Sizes and Specs
Nitto Trail Grappler Product Page

summary: The JL Rubicon is the only Wrangler that fits 37s from the factory without modification — and even on the Rubicon you will get occasional flex rubbing. On every other JL trim, 37s require a lift and a plan.
description:
Jeep was deliberate about the JL Rubicon's tire clearance. The Rubicon comes with a 1" front lift, wider fender flares, and 33" tires from the factory — but the geometry allows for 37s with minimal clearance work at full flex. In practice, 37s on a stock Rubicon rub at full steering lock combined with full bump travel. The rub points are the front upper control arm at the coil bucket and the rear fender liner at full droop. Most Rubicon owners address this with a 1"–1.5" spacer lift or minor fender liner trimming without a full kit.

Non-Rubicon JL trim levels (Sport, Sport S, Sahara) are a different situation. The factory fender openings are narrower, the suspension geometry is lower, and the tires are 31"–33" from the factory. Fitting 37s without a lift results in rubbing at every steering and suspension extreme — you need 2.5" of lift minimum, and 3.5" is the more comfortable clearance baseline. At 2.5" you will still need fender liner removal (not cutting, just pulling the liner) at the rear, and the front upper control arm area needs attention at full steering lock. At 3.5", 37s fit cleanly across all four corners.

The tire choices matter for fitment as much as the size. A 37x12.5R17 is the most common spec, and all three recommended options here are in that range. Note that actual measured width varies by brand — the BFG KM3 at 37x12.5 measures close to nominal, the Nitto Trail Grappler runs slightly narrower, and the Toyo Open Country MT runs slightly wider depending on the wheel backspacing. On a 17x8.5 or 17x9 wheel with 4.5"–5" backspace, all three mount cleanly.

**Regear is not optional at 37s.** Stock gear ratios on the Sahara (3.45) and Sport (3.73) were engineered around 31"–33" tires. Adding 37s effectively drops your RPM at highway speed and loads the drivetrain heavily off-road. The Sahara with 3.45 gears and 37s is genuinely painful to drive — low-end torque evaporates, the transmission hunts gears on grades, and trail crawl ratios are inadequate. Plan for 4.56 gears with 35s, 4.88 gears with 37s on Sahara/Sport. Rubicon owners with the 4.10 stock ratio can run 37s tolerable, but 4.56 is the right answer for serious trail use.

**TPMS:** The JL uses a direct TPMS system — sensors in each wheel. When you move to aftermarket wheels, the sensors must either be transferred from factory wheels or new sensors purchased and programmed. TPMS sensors for the JL are vehicle-specific; verify compatibility before ordering.
steps: If installing new wheels alongside new tires, mount tires on new wheels at a tire shop — spec 4.5"–5" backspacing for lifted JL builds.
Verify TPMS sensors are transferred or new compatible sensors are installed before mounting.
Lift the vehicle on jack stands and remove factory wheels.
Install new wheel/tire assemblies. Torque lug nuts to 100 ft-lb in a star pattern.
Lower the vehicle and re-torque after 50 miles.
Turn steering wheel to full lock in both directions and articulate suspension through full travel (ramp or spotter needed for this) to check for rub points.
If rubbing is present: identify the location and address — rear fender liner removal is a 20-minute task, front upper control arm rub may require trim cutting or a minor lift correction.
If no regear is yet planned, reset tire size in the vehicle's computer (speedometer calibration). JL uses the Uconnect system; some builds use a programmer or dealer reflash for this.
pros: 37s are the meaningful capability threshold for serious trail work — more traction footprint, more ground clearance, better over-rock rollover
On the Rubicon, the modification scope is genuinely minor — the vehicle was designed to accommodate them
BFG KM3, Nitto Trail Grappler, and Toyo OPMT are all proven tires with extensive JL trail-use history
Proper 37s make the JL look proportional — the body was designed with large tires in mind
cons: Non-Rubicon fitment requires 2.5"+ lift — that cost is additive to the tire cost
Regear is functionally required on Sport (3.73) and Sahara (3.45) — budget an additional $1,800–$2,400 for a proper gear change
37s are heavy — rotating mass increase affects acceleration, braking, and fuel economy noticeably
TPMS sensor compatibility requires verification for aftermarket wheels; factory sensors may need reprogramming
A full set of 37s plus a quality wheel set plus regear is a $4,000–$5,000 package total — budget realistically

title: Wheel Selection for the JL — Steel, Alloy, and Beadlock

parts.name: Pro Comp Series 31 Steel Wheel 17x9 -6mm offset

citations.title: Method Race Wheels 305 NV Fitment Guide
Fuel Off-Road D533 Boost Wheel Specs
KMC Machete Crawl Beadlock Overview

summary: The JL uses a 5x127 (5x5") bolt pattern and needs 4.5"–5" of backspacing on most lifted builds — get those two numbers right and the wheel selection becomes straightforward.
description:
Wheel selection for the JL is primarily a function of bolt pattern, backspacing, and use case. The bolt pattern is fixed: 5x127mm (often called 5x5"). Backspacing determines how far the wheel face sits inside the fender relative to the wheel centerline — too much backspace and the tire tucks too far under the fender, creating clearance issues on a lifted rig; too little and the tire pokes out beyond the fender flares, requiring flare extensions or risking legality issues in some states. For a lifted JL running 35"–37" tires, 4.5"–5" backspacing puts the tire face at the fender edge on most builds.

Steel wheels (Pro Comp Series 31 at $95 each) are the right call for builds where rock contact is expected. Steel deforms on impact rather than cracking, which means a bent steel wheel is usually fixable trailside with a hammer and a tire iron while a cracked alloy wheel is not. The Pro Comp Series 31 is a functional, no-frills 17x9 in the correct backspace for JL trail use. At $95 per wheel, replacing a badly damaged one isn't catastrophic.

The Method 305 NV at $175 per wheel is the benchmark alloy option. Method's NV (No Void) design eliminates spokes entirely, which means no stress concentrations at spoke roots — the common failure point on spoke-design alloy wheels. The face is a machined flat disc. It's heavier than spoked alloys but more impact-resistant. Method's quality control is consistent and their 17x8.5 0mm offset works well on lifted JL builds. This is a popular choice because it's functional on the trail and looks reasonable on the street.

The Fuel Boost D533 at $185 per wheel is the value alloy option with a more aggressive aesthetic. The offset (-12mm) provides slightly more tire clearance than the Method on non-Rubicon fenders. Fuel's construction quality is solid for the price point, and the D533 is widely available.

The KMC Machete Crawl Beadlock at $320 per wheel is the choice for builds that run reduced tire pressure on technical terrain. Beadlock wheels clamp the tire bead mechanically, preventing tire de-beading at low pressures (12–20 psi range). The KMC unit is a two-piece design with an inner ring that can be retorqued periodically — correct maintenance is required. DOT-approved beadlocks don't exist in the traditional sense; the Machete Crawl is labeled for off-road use only, which has legal implications for street use in some states.

**TPMS:** The JL uses a direct TPMS system. When changing to aftermarket wheels, your factory TPMS sensors must be transferred by a tire shop (requires proper tools) or replaced with aftermarket sensors verified for JL compatibility. Budget $15–$20 per sensor for new ones if not reusing factory sensors.
steps: Transfer or install TPMS sensors onto new wheels before mounting tires. This is done at a tire shop with a sensor programming tool.
Mount tires onto new wheels at the tire shop, specifying the correct mounting torque for bead seating.

For beadlock wheels (KMC Machete Crawl): the outer ring must be installed with the tire, with ring bolt torque set to spec and re-checked at first install — consult the KMC installation instructions for bolt pattern and torque spec.
Lift the vehicle on jack stands, remove factory wheels.
Install new wheel/tire assemblies. Torque lug nuts to 100 ft-lb in a star pattern.
Lower vehicle and re-torque lug nuts after 50 miles.
Confirm backspacing clearance at full steering lock and full flex — look for rubbing at the inner fender liner, upper control arm, and spring perch.
pros: Method 305 NV's no-void design is the most impact-resistant alloy option in this price range
Steel wheels (Pro Comp) are the practical choice for builds that regularly contact rocks — cheaper to replace than alloys
KMC Machete Crawl beadlocks enable low-pressure trail operation that dramatically improves rock-crawl traction
Correct backspacing on all listed options for lifted JL builds — no wheel spacers required
All options listed cover the full 5x127 bolt pattern JL requirement
cons: TPMS sensor transfer or replacement adds $60–$100 to the wheel cost and requires a shop visit
Beadlock wheels (KMC) require periodic ring bolt torque checks — not a set-and-forget install
Alloy wheels (Method, Fuel) crack rather than deform on severe impact — a cracked alloy wheel ends the trail day
Steel wheels are heavy — rotating mass from steel wheels is measurably higher than alloys, affecting acceleration and fuel economy
Backspacing should be confirmed against your specific lift height and tire width before ordering — published specs are starting points, not guarantees
